name: Major Historical Events
subtitle: The full chronology of the Half-Made World, from creation to the present day
description:
The history of the Half-Made World is measured in the Veyn Calendar (VC). Year 0 is the Sundering — the moment the Hidden Realm was created and the world was nearly destroyed. All dates before the Sundering are approximate and debated. The current year is approximately 2350 VC.

---

THE TIMELINE

■ THE AGE OF THE AELTHAR (Before Year 0 — exact duration unknown)

The Aelthar were the original ruling race of the world — ancient beings of pure Veyn energy who shaped reality itself. They built the world as a garden, filled it with life, and walked among their creations. During their reign:

  • The Aelthar built the Shudon — stone golems made from world-core material — to guard the realm entrances and regulate the flow of Veyn across the world.
  • The Aelthar discovered the World Eater — a parasitic consciousness embedded in the world core, slowly draining its power over centuries. The World Eater was not a creature born of Veyn; it existed outside it, converting pure world-core Veyn into null-Veyn, an absence of magical energy.
  • The Shudon were originally designed not just as realm guardians but as core regulators, built to detect and suppress the World Eater's spread.
  • The Aelthar began developing the technology to create a Hidden Realm — an artificial refuge that would redirect the World Eater's feeding away from the main core and provide an escape for the survivors.
  • The Aelthar wrote the Sealed Writings — approximately 50 texts containing their knowledge, each protected by a Veyn seal that only opens for someone with Aelthar-level Veyn sensitivity.
  • The Aelthar also wrote the Prophecy of the Half-Made — a stone tablet etched in Old Aelthar script, warning of a being who would be "half-made" and face a choice between mending and destroying the Sundering.

Duration of the Aelthar Age: Unknown. Some scholars believe it lasted tens of thousands of years. Others argue it was shorter — perhaps only a few thousand. The Aelthar themselves left no precise record of their own beginning.

---

■ THE SUNDERING (Year 0)

The single most catastrophic event in the world's history. When the Hidden Realm was forcefully created, the resulting Veyn disruption nearly destroyed the world entirely.

  • The creation of the Hidden Realm drew power from the world core, creating a massive Veyn disruption that split reality itself.
  • The world barrier was made — a metaphysical boundary that split the world into the three main realms (Human, Angel, Demon) and the Hidden Realm, preventing the destruction from spreading further.
  • The Void Colossus appeared at the breach point — a towering humanoid figure of compressed void energy, thirty to fifty feet tall, attacking everything nearby. It is a projection of the void's own immune response, drawn to any breach in the realm barrier.
  • The Aelthar were wiped out in the conflict. The Echoes of the Fallen — spiritual imprints of Aelthar warriors — still fight on the battlefield in the Shattered Lands, trapped in a loop of their final stand.
  • The Hidden Realm formed around the survivors. Within it, all sorts of creatures began to form spontaneously from the unstable Veyn. The Aelthar survivors, not knowing how to hunt these creatures, all died except one: the Head Master of the Academy, who alone learned to endure the realm and later became the only person to ever successfully brew the Ethereal Potion.
  • The Shudon became inactive following the Sundering — their connection to the world core was disrupted by the barrier's creation. No one currently knows how to reactivate them.
  • The World Barrier sealed the realms apart. Each realm developed its own culture, races, and power structures in isolation.
  • The Veyn Storms began — unpredictable surges of Veyn that disrupted the natural order across all three realms.
  • The Echoes of the Sundering began manifesting across all three realms — spatial anomalies, temporal glitches, emotional imprints, and material distortions that continue to this day.

Aftermath: The world was broken into three realms plus the Hidden Realm. The Aelthar were gone. The Shudon were silent. The World Eater continued to drain the world core, now unchecked. And the survivors — scattered, terrified, and leaderless — began the long process of rebuilding.

---

■ THE FIRST TURNING (Year 500)

The first recurrence of the Sundering Prophecy Cycle — the pattern where a major event occurs every 500 years that either heals or damages the boundaries between realms.

  • The Veil formed — the Hidden Realm was sealed away more completely, its portal becoming unstable and relocating every leap year. The Veil is the barrier that separates the Hidden Realm from the other three.
  • The Sealed Writings scattered — the 50 Aelthar texts, originally kept in one location, were dispersed across all three realms during the upheaval. No one knows who scattered them or why.
  • The first Veyn Storms of note occurred in the Human Realm, causing localized destruction and creating the first Veyn-Dead Zones.

Significance: The first turning established the pattern that would repeat every 500 years. It also sealed the Hidden Realm away, trapping the surviving Aelthar (later just Kael) inside.

---

■ THE HUMAN RISE (Years 800–1200)

With the Aelthar gone and the Shudon inactive, humanity expanded rapidly. This period saw the formation of the current three-realm political structure.

  • The unnamed Human Realm ruler began a campaign of conquest, expanding human territory across what would become the Human Realm.
  • The Human Realm ruler killed off most of the survivors of the Hidden Realm creation — those Aelthar and other beings who had escaped the Sundering but had not yet entered the Hidden Realm. This was a deliberate genocide, motivated by fear of the Aelthar's power and a desire to eliminate any threat to human dominance.
  • The Angel Realm and Demon Realm consolidated their own territories during this period, establishing the borders that exist today.
  • The Ether Forest — the forest split into light (Arubian) and dark (Umbrage) halves — became the contested border zone between the Human and Demon Realms.
  • The Pallantine Elves settled in the Arubian Forest. The Veilborn Elves settled in the Umbrage Forest. The two elven groups, originally one race, diverged culturally and politically.
  • The Broker's Guild was founded — originally a small mediation office handling cross-realm contracts, it would grow into the most powerful neutral institution in the world.

Duration: Approximately 400 years of gradual expansion and consolidation.

---

■ THE SECOND TURNING (Year 1000)

The second recurrence of the Sundering Prophecy Cycle.

  • The First Realm Gate was created — a permanent stone arch connecting the Human Realm and Angel Realm. This was the first stable passage between realms since the Sundering.
  • The Realm Gates allowed formal cross-realm travel for the first time, enabling trade, diplomacy, and cultural exchange.
  • The Angel Realm opened its borders slightly — Lumen began traveling to the Human Realm, and the first Angel-Human diplomatic exchanges occurred.
  • The Demon Realm remained sealed — no Demon Realm gate was created, and demons continued to isolate themselves.

Significance: The second turning began the slow process of reconnecting the broken realms. It also established the pattern of the Angel Realm being more open to connection than the Demon Realm.

---

■ THE FOUNDING OF ELYNDOR ACADEMY (Year ~1300–1500)

Kael von Ashen, the last surviving Aelthar, emerged from the Hidden Realm and founded Elyndor Academy using recovered Aelthar knowledge.

  • Kael built both Sundering Altars — the Common Altar in a neutral temple between the three realms, and the Academy Altar within Elyndor Academy itself. Both altars channel Veyn from the world core to awaken latent magical abilities in children at age 15.
  • The Academy established the magical awakening system that exists today — every child of every race is brought to the Academy at age 15 to undergo their awakening.
  • The Veyn Calendar was standardized by the Academy, giving all three realms a common dating system.
  • The Academy established its neutrality — it serves all three realms equally, providing education and magical training without political allegiance.
  • The Grade System was formalized — G through S grades, with sub-stages, providing a standardized measure of magical ability.
  • The Class System was formalized — 18 classes with defined skill trees and progression paths.
  • The Sundering Altars were built using Aelthar knowledge and world-core Veyn, making them the only reliable way to awaken magic.

Note: The exact date of the Academy's founding is debated. Some records suggest it was closer to 1500 years ago; others place it more recently. Kael von Ashen, as the last Aelthar, is extraordinarily long-lived — his exact age is unknown, but he has served as Head Master for centuries.

---

■ THE THIRD TURNING (Year 1500)

The third recurrence of the Sundering Prophecy Cycle.

  • The Demon Realm expanded — demonic territory grew by approximately 20%, pushing into previously neutral zones. This expansion was aggressive and contested, leading to border conflicts with both the Human and Angel Realms.
  • The Obsidian Spires were established as the Demon Realm's capital during this period.
  • The Demon Clans began their shift from scattered war-bands to organized political units, setting the stage for the Unification Wars.
  • The Angel Realm reinforced its borders in response to the Demon expansion, beginning the period of Angel isolationism that would deepen during the Civil War.

Significance: The third turning was the most violent of the three, directly causing territorial changes and setting up the political tensions that persist today.

---

■ THE FIRST VEYN STORM CATASTROPHE (Year ~1350)

The largest Veyn Storm in recorded history struck the central Human Realm.

  • The storm lasted 72 hours and covered an area of 1,000 miles.
  • 10,000+ casualties from uncontrolled Veyn manifestation.
  • Permanent Veyn-Dead Zones created across 200 miles of territory.
  • Spontaneous Corrupted Veyn outbreaks occurred, creating the first Corruption Scars.
  • Several Aelthar ruins were temporarily activated, releasing ancient constructs and traps.
  • The catastrophe led to: the founding of the Academy's Veyn Storm monitoring program, the construction of Veyn-dampened shelters in all major cities, and the Pallantine Rangers' mandate to maintain early-warning systems.

Significance: The First Catastrophe demonstrated that the Sundering's damage was not just historical — it was ongoing and worsening.

---

■ THE ANGEL CIVIL WAR (Years ~1550–1580)

A devastating 30-year civil war within the Angel Realm between the Purity Faction (who believed Angels should remain isolated) and the Outreach Faction (who believed Angels should interact with other realms).

  • The war killed approximately 30% of the Angel population — a catastrophic loss for a race that barely breeds.
  • The Purity Faction ultimately won, but at such severe cost that the Angel Realm withdrew from cross-realm politics for centuries.
  • The Angel Echo Network was redesigned to prevent political dissent from spreading.
  • Angel promise culture became even more conservative — fewer promises, more careful consideration.
  • Angel isolationism deepened, creating the diplomatic tensions that persist today.

Significance: The Civil War explains why the Angel Realm is so insular and why Clint Ashborn rules with such absolute authority — the trauma of a civilization that nearly destroyed itself made angels desperate for order.

---

■ THE PROPHETIC TABLET DISCOVERED (Year ~1550)

During the aftermath of the Angel Civil War, the Seer's Order discovered the stone tablet containing the Prophecy of the Half-Made, buried beneath rubble in the Shattered Lands.

  • The tablet was written in Old Aelthar script — a language no living being could fully read.
  • The Seer's Order spent centuries attempting to translate it, producing a version that is widely accepted but acknowledged to be incomplete (15-20% lost or illegible).
  • The prophecy spoke of a "Half-Made" being who would face a choice: "the seam or the silence."
  • The Seer's Order began quietly searching for the Half-Made — a search that would last centuries without success.
  • Different factions interpreted the prophecy differently: Angels saw it as a path to restoration, Demons saw it as a threat, Humans saw it as a reason to prepare.

Significance: The prophecy became the hidden thread running through all cross-realm politics — every faction knew about it, and every faction had a plan for when the Half-Made appeared.

---

■ THE DEMON UNIFICATION WARS (Years ~1950–1965)

A 15-year series of brutal wars in which the Demon Realm was unified under a single ruler.

  • Before unification, demons fought each other as much as other races. 60 Demon Clans existed, constantly warring.
  • The Unification Wars eliminated or absorbed 40 of the 60 Clans. The surviving 20 Clans form the current Demon power structure.
  • The wars established: the Obsidian Spires as the Demon capital, the Pit as the formal challenge system, the Great Clans as political units, and the Demon military doctrine of overwhelming force.
  • The wars also created the Wound — a 10-mile-long, 2-mile-wide Corruption Scar near the Demon Realm border, created when a Demon Lord used a massive Corrupted Veyn weapon. The Wound is so toxic that even demons avoid it.
  • The current Mordrach (Tera Morage) rose to power during or shortly after the Unification Wars, tearing the crown from the king before her.

Significance: The Unification Wars created the Demon Realm as it exists today — a militarized, hierarchical society where power is seized through violence and maintained through fear.

---

■ THE BROKEN CROWN REBELLION (Year ~2150)

A military coup attempt within the Human Realm that nearly toppled the monarchy.

  • Aldric Thornwall, a Human noble commanding three Trading Houses and half the Realm Army's Iron Division, attempted to seize the Crown.
  • The rebellion lasted 6 months: Aldric captured the capital, declared himself King, and was eventually defeated by a coalition of loyalist forces, Pallantine Rangers, and an Angel diplomatic intervention.
  • The rebellion's legacy: the Crown Advisory Council was reformed to include non-military representatives, the Iron Division was split into smaller units, and the Broker's Guild gained expanded authority.
  • Current succession law includes a provision: the ruler cannot be under 16 years of age.

Significance: The Broken Crown Rebellion demonstrated that even the most stable realm could fracture — and that external intervention (Angels, Broker's Guild) was sometimes necessary to preserve order.

---

■ THE ANGEL-HUMAN TRADE ACCORD (Year ~2250)

A formal trade agreement between the Angel Realm and Human Realm, regulated by the Broker's Guild.

  • Covers Sunveil Silk and Veyn Crystal exchange.
  • Reviewed every 10 years.
  • The most stable cross-realm agreement, though it remains fragile.
  • The Human-Demon "Informal Understanding" (unofficial trade through intermediaries) operates alongside it, though both sides pretend not to know.

Significance: The Accord represents the best-case scenario for cross-realm cooperation — and its fragility represents the constant risk of collapse.

---

■ THE PRESENT ERA (Year ~2350 VC)

The current state of the world, as the story begins.

  • The three realms exist in a tense peace enforced by the Academy's neutrality.
  • The Shudon remain inactive — no one knows how to reactivate them.
  • The World Eater continues to drain the world core, slowly and silently.
  • The Hidden Realm portal moves every leap year, drawing in ambient Veyn until it can relocate.
  • The Sundering Prophecy Cycle is approaching its fourth turning (expected around Year 2500).
  • The Seer's Order has spent centuries searching for the Half-Made without success.
  • Dark Moon, led by the fallen angel Wener Leger, is building power in the shadows.
  • Licent Varak, Tera Morage's second right-hand, is secretly allied with Dark Moon.
  • Ruby Divina, the mortal ruler of the Human Realm, knows about Jaiden Marlock and has been shielding him as humanity's leverage.
  • Clint Ashborn, the Serapharch, has ordered the execution of his own right-hand man for fathering a hybrid child — and the child survived.
  • Kael von Ashen, the last Aelthar and Head Master of the Academy, is preparing to take a student to the Hidden Realm.
  • And somewhere in the Human Realm, a boy named Jaiden Marlock — the first Angel-Demon Hybrid in the world's history — is about to turn 15.

What comes next is not written in any prophecy. It is written by the choices of the people who live in this broken, beautiful, half-made world.

name: Festivals & Holidays
subtitle: The public celebrations observed across all three realms
description:
Five Festival Days occur between each month, with an extra Day of Renewal at year's end. These are public holidays observed across all three realms, though each realm celebrates them differently.

The Day of Awakening (between months 1 and 2): Celebrates the children who turned 15 in Awakening Month and received their classes. Families feast, and the newly awakened demonstrate their first skills for their communities.

The Bloom Festival (between months 2 and 3): A celebration of spring and growth. In the Human Realm, farmers plant ceremonial first seeds. In the Angel Realm, angels hang golden lanterns from their halos. In the Demon Realm, demons share food with strangers — one of the few days demons are genuinely friendly.

The Shatter Remembrance (between months 6 and 7): A solemn day of silence commemorating the destruction of the Aelthar. All three realms observe a moment of silence at noon. The Echoes of the Fallen battlefield glows brighter on this day.

The Veil Night (between months 7 and 8): When the Ether Forest boundary is thinnest, creatures from both halves mingle. It is considered bad luck to enter the forest on this night, but many do anyway to collect rare ingredients that only appear during the Veil.

The Day of Sundering (between months 9 and 10): The most significant holiday — commemorates the creation of the Hidden Realm and the near-destruction of the world. All three realms hold ceremonies at their respective Sundering Altars. The Academy holds a special demonstration of the Altar's power.

The Renewal Feast (year's end): A grand celebration where debts are forgiven, feuds are set aside, and everyone feasts regardless of rank or race. It is the one night when the Demon Realm's marketplace is genuinely festive rather than dangerous.

name: Realm Travel Methods
subtitle: How people move between the three main realms
description:
Travel between the three main realms follows established paths through the world barrier — the invisible boundary that separates the realms and prevents casual crossing.

The primary method of realm crossing is through the Realm Gates — large, permanent stone arches located at the borders of each realm. There are three Realm Gates: one at the Human Realm border, one at the Angel Realm border, and one at the Demon Realm border. Each is guarded by a Shudon (currently inactive, which is why the gates function without obstruction).

When the Shudon are active, the gates will require authorization to pass — anyone bearing the world curse mark will be attacked, and unauthorized crossing will be blocked. For now, anyone can walk through, though the transition is disorienting: a brief flash of Veyn distortion, a sensation of falling, and then you're in the next realm.

The Hidden Realm cannot be reached through Realm Gates. Its only entrance is the wandering portal, which moves every leap year by drawing in ambient Veyn until it can relocate. Predicting where the portal will appear requires sensing Veyn density — someone with a strong enough sense of Veyn density could theoretically predict roughly where it might appear next.

Within each realm, travel follows standard medieval methods: roads, horses, Griffens (for Pallantine Elves), and on foot. The Sunward Road between the Human and Angel Realms is well-maintained and safe. The Thorn Road between the Human and Demon Realms is dangerous and requires hired guards.

name: Road Network & Infrastructure
subtitle: The paths and stops that connect settlements
description:
The Half-Made World has a network of roads maintained by each realm's government, though quality varies dramatically.

The Human Realm has the most developed road network. The Sunward Road is the crown jewel — a wide, paved road connecting the capital to the Angel Realm border, lined with waystones every mile. Side roads connect major cities and towns, maintained by local lords who tax merchants for their use. The roads are patrolled by human soldiers, and roadside inns appear every 20-30 miles — roughly a day's travel for a caravan.

The Angel Realm has fewer roads but better ones. Angel roads are built from Veyn-infused stone that resists weathering and glows faintly at night, making night travel safe. The roads connect the major angel cities but are rarely used by non-angels — most travelers find the glowing stones unsettling.

The Demon Realm has almost no roads. Demons travel by trail, instinct, and territorial knowledge. The Umbrage Forest has no paths — anyone entering must navigate by Veyn sense or follow the rare markers left by Gnash traders. This makes the Demon Realm the most dangerous to travel through.

Roadside infrastructure includes inns, taverns, blacksmiths, and general stores in the Human Realm. In the Angel Realm, waystation shelters appear along major routes — simple stone buildings with beds, water, and basic supplies, maintained by Lumen volunteers. The Demon Realm has nothing — you sleep where you stop, or you don't sleep at all.

name: Communication & News
subtitle: How information travels across the realms
description:
In the Half-Made World, news travels at the speed of the fastest available messenger — which varies dramatically by realm.

The primary method of long-distance communication is through trained messenger birds called Swiftwings — small, fast birds that can carry messages across realms. Each realm maintains its own Swiftwing corps. The Human Realm's Swiftwings are the most numerous, with relay stations every 50 miles along major roads. A message from the Human Realm capital to the Angel Realm border takes roughly two days via Swiftwing relay.

The Angel Realm uses a more elegant system: Lumen messengers who can fly. A Lumen carrying a message can cover the distance between Angel cities in hours rather than days. The problem is that Lumen messengers are rare — most Lumen are civilians who don't want to serve as postal workers.

The Demon Realm has no formal communication system. Demons rely on rumor, word-of-mouth, and the Gnash trader network. News travels fast in the Demon Realm because demons gossip relentlessly, but accuracy is low. A rumor that starts as 'there's trouble in the Umbrage' can become 'the world is ending' within a day.

The Academy maintains its own communication network — a series of enchanted mirrors that allow instant communication between the Academy and each realm's ruler. This is the fastest communication method in the world, but it is strictly limited to Academy-ruler correspondence. Using the mirrors for personal communication is forbidden.

Newspapers, books, and printed materials are rare. Books are hand-copied by scribes and are expensive luxury items. The Academy maintains the largest library in the world, but access is restricted to students and faculty.

name: Lodging & Rest Stops
subtitle: Where travelers sleep and rest across the realms
description:
Travelers in the Half-Made World have varying options for rest depending on the realm they're in.

In the Human Realm, inns and taverns are the standard accommodation. Every town has at least one inn, and major crossroads have several competing establishments. A bed in a shared room costs 5 cp; a private room costs 1 sm; a luxury suite at a high-end inn costs 1 gc. Inns typically serve food and drink as well, making them one-stop shops for travelers. The best-known inn chain is the Resting Stone network — a series of identical inns along the Sunward Road, each offering the same menu and prices regardless of location.

The Angel Realm has waystation shelters along major routes — simple stone buildings with beds, water, and basic supplies, maintained by Lumen volunteers. These are free to use but offer no food or luxury. For angels traveling to other realms, the Angel Realm maintains guest houses in the Human Realm's capital, provided free of charge to any angel showing Dawnveil.

The Demon Realm has nothing for travelers. Demons sleep in the wild, in caves, or in the homes of those they trust. Gnash traders sometimes offer shelter to those willing to pay Gold Crowns, but this comes with strings attached — a Gnash who shelters you expects a favor in return.

The Hidden Realm offers no permanent lodging. The time-slowed environment means travelers don't need to eat or sleep as often, but there are no structures built for comfort. The Wanderer occasionally appears and offers shelter, but always at a price.

name: Criminal Code
subtitle: The crimes and punishments of the Half-Made World
description:
The Half-Made World recognizes several categories of crime, each with different punishments depending on severity and realm.

Crimes Against Persons: Assault, murder, kidnapping, and forced Veyn/Ren tampering (interfering with someone's channels without consent). Murder carries the harshest penalty — death or permanent channel severing, depending on the realm. Assault carries fines and imprisonment.

Crimes Against Property: Theft, trespassing, and fraud. Theft of under 1 Gold Crown is punished with public flogging and repayment. Theft over 1 Gold Crown is imprisonment. Theft of magical items or artifacts is treated as a national security crime — the accused is handed to the Exorcists for Veyn interrogation.

Crimes Against the State: Treason, rebellion, assassination attempts, and unauthorized realm crossing. These are punished by death in all three realms. The Angel Realm adds public Vow-shaming — the criminal's broken Vow is broadcast to nearby angels.

Crimes Against Magic: Illegal enchantment, forced awakening tampering, and unsanctioned use of the Sundering Altar. These are handled exclusively by the Academy, and punishment ranges from channel severing to exile from all three realms.

Contract Fraud: Breaking a Broker-sealed contract is a unique crime — the physical damage to the breaker's channels serves as both punishment and evidence. The Broker's Guild prosecutes these cases.

name: Law Enforcement
subtitle: The systems that maintain order across realms
description:
Each realm enforces its own laws differently.

The Human Realm has the most structured law enforcement. Every city has a Magistrate — a D-rank or higher appointed by Ruby Divina — who oversees local justice. Below the Magistrate are Wardens, armed officers who patrol cities and towns. Wardens are typically F-rank fighters with basic combat training. Serious crimes (murder, magical crimes) are escalated to the Magistrate, who may call in Exorcists or consult the Academy.

The Angel Realm relies on the Virtue class for law enforcement. Angel law is simpler — most crimes are settled through Vow-shaming or community judgment. Serious crimes are brought before the Serapharch directly. There is no formal police force; angels police themselves through social pressure and Vow accountability.

The Demon Realm has no formal law enforcement. Justice is enforced by the strong against the weak. Bloodwards maintain order in major settlements through fear and force. Gnash demons are expected to resolve disputes through combat or contract. The concept of 'law' as humans understand it doesn't exist — only power hierarchies.

The Academy has its own internal security: Instructors who double as peacekeepers. They handle crimes committed by students or within Academy grounds. The Head Master has final authority on all Academy matters.

name: Trial by Combat
subtitle: Settling disputes through sanctioned fighting
description:
Trial by Combat is a legal method of dispute resolution recognized in all three realms, though practiced differently in each.

In the Human Realm, Trial by Combat is available when evidence is insufficient for a normal trial. The accused may challenge their accuser to a fight — if the accused wins, they are declared innocent. If they lose, guilt is confirmed. The fight is overseen by a Magistrate and must follow strict rules: no killing unless both parties agree, no use of magical items or artifacts, and the fight ends when one party yields or is unable to continue.

In the Angel Realm, Trial by Combat is called a Vow Duel — both parties swear a Vow that the outcome will be accepted as truth. Because breaking a Vow has physical consequences, angels rarely invoke this unless they are certain of their innocence. The Serapharch or an Aetherblade Lord presides.

In the Demon Realm, Trial by Combat is the ONLY form of justice. There are no courts, no Magistrates, no evidence. If you are accused, you fight your accuser. The survivor is deemed right. This applies to everything from theft to murder to contract disputes.

The Broker's Guild prohibits Trial by Combat for contract disputes — sealed contracts are binding regardless of combat outcomes.

name: Smuggling & Black Market
subtitle: The underground economy of the Half-Made World
description:
Smuggling is a thriving underground economy, especially along the Thorn Road between the Human and Demon Realms.

The most commonly smuggled goods are corrupted Veyn artifacts — items imbued with demonic miasma that are illegal in the Human Realm but valuable on the black market. Exorcists actively hunt smugglers of these items because corrupted Veyn can trigger Corruption Sickness in anyone who handles it carelessly.

Pixie dust is another high-value smuggled item. Because it can only be obtained in the Hidden Realm and is extremely rare, a single pouch of pixie dust can sell for 50+ Gold Crowns on the black market — ten times what it would cost through legitimate channels if legitimate channels existed.

The Demon Realm's Umbrage Forest border is the primary smuggling corridor. Gnash traders operate the network, moving goods through hidden paths that bypass the official Thorn Road checkpoints. The Broker's Guild knows about the smuggling but tolerates it as long as it doesn't involve contract fraud or corrupted artifacts that could destabilize realm relations.

Information is also smuggled — secrets about realm politics, military movements, and Academy research are traded between realms by rogue scholars and disgruntled officials. The most valuable intelligence is information about the Shudon — any detail about how to reactivate them is worth a fortune.

name: Assassination & Bounty Contracts
subtitle: The organized killing trade
description:
Assassination exists in the Half-Made World but is not openly practiced — it is channeled through the Broker's Guild as 'termination contracts.'

A termination contract is a Broker-sealed agreement where a client pays a specified sum for the death of a target. The Broker is legally required to verify that the target is not protected by any realm authority (ruling families, Academy staff, Six Pillars members, etc.). Contracting the death of a protected individual is treated as treason.

The Guild maintains a roster of approved contractors — Veilrunners and high-rank Berserkers who have passed additional ethical screenings (ironic for assassins, but the Guild maintains standards). Contractors are paid upon completion, with the Broker holding the payment in escrow until the contract is fulfilled.

Bounty contracts are separate — these are public warrants issued by Magistrates for the capture (dead or alive) of criminals. Bounties are posted in taverns and marketplaces. The amount varies by the criminal's grade and the severity of their crimes. A common thief might carry a 5 Silver Mark bounty; a rogue Exorcist could carry a 50 Gold Crown bounty.

The Demon Realm has no restrictions on assassination — anyone can hire a Gnash to kill anyone else, provided the Gnash accepts the contract.

name: The World Core Faith
subtitle: The deity system of the Half-Made World — who or what the races worship
description:
The Half-Made World does not have a traditional pantheon of gods. Instead, it has a single supreme entity — the World Core — and a web of theological disagreements about what it is, whether it is conscious, and what it wants. Every race interprets the World Core differently, and those interpretations shape everything from daily worship to military strategy.

---

THE DIVINE HIERARCHY

1. THE WORLD CORE — The Sleeping God

The World Core is the source of all Veyn, the animator of all life, and the force that holds the realms together. It exists beneath the world's crust, radiating Veyn outward through ley lines that branch into every realm. Whether it is conscious is the central theological question of the world.

Three interpretations exist:

  • The Human View (The Dreamer): The World Core is a living entity that fell asleep before recorded history. It dreams the world into existence — every sunrise, every season, every life is part of its dream. When it wakes, the dream ends. Humans worship it by creating (planting, building, healing) because creation sustains the dream. Destruction disturbs it.

  • The Angel View (The Arbiter): The World Core is conscious but impartial — it watches every Vow, every promise, every oath, and judges them. It does not sleep; it discerns. Angels believe the halo is the Core's seal of approval — a physical proof that the world accepted the angel's promise. Breaking a Vow is not just a personal failure; it is a breach of trust with the entity that holds reality together.

  • The Demon View (The Fuel): The World Core is a resource, not a god. It produces Veyn the way a mine produces ore — without intent, without consciousness, without care. Demons see worship of the Core as weakness. They take what they need by force. The Core does not reward or punish; it simply exists, and the strong are those who take the most from it.

  • The Aelthar View (The Architect — extinct, recovered from lore): The World Core is the original creator — not a god in the religious sense, but a force of such magnitude that the difference is academic. The Aelthar believed the Core shaped the world intentionally, then withdrew into dormancy to let its creation evolve. The Core's "dream" is not unconscious — it is a deliberate act of observation. The Aelthar built the Shudon as the Core's maintenance system, and the Core permitted it.

2. THE AELTHAR — The Shaped Ones (Extinct)

The Aelthar were not gods, but they were the closest thing to divine beings the world has ever produced. Created by the World Core (or born from it, depending on interpretation), they understood Veyn at a fundamental level and used that understanding to shape reality. They built the Shudon, discovered the World Eater, and created the Hidden Realm.

In human theology, the Aelthar are remembered as "the first children" — beings who were given divine power and squandered it through hubris. The Aelthar Creation Myth teaches that the Aelthar grew proud and tried to control the Veyn itself, causing the Sundering. This myth is used as a cautionary tale: power without wisdom destroys.

In angel theology, the Aelthar are revered as the original architects of the Vow system — the beings who first understood that promises could be made binding through Veyn. Angels believe the Aelthar's downfall was not hubris but sacrifice — they tore open the Hidden Realm to save the world from the World Eater, and the cost was their own extinction.

In demon theology, the Aelthar are irrelevant. They existed, they died, their Veyn returned to the Core. End of story.

3. THE SHUDON — The Hands of God

The Shudon are not gods, but they are the closest thing to divine instruments in the world. Built by the Aelthar from world-core material, they were designed to maintain balance and guard against disturbances. Their current inactivity is interpreted differently by each race:

  • Humans: The Shudon are sleeping because the Core is sleeping. When the Core wakes, the Shudon will reawaken.
  • Angels: The Shudon are waiting for a promise worthy of their service. When an angel speaks a Vow powerful enough, the Shudon will respond.
  • Demons: The Shudon are broken. The Aelthar built them wrong, and they failed. Nothing built by the dead is worth respecting.
  • World Core Faith: The Shudon are the Core's immune system — they activate when the Core detects a threat. Their inactivity means the World Eater has not yet crossed the threshold of danger.

4. THE WORLD EATER — The Anti-God

The World Eater is not a deity, but it functions as the inverse of one — a parasitic consciousness that drains the Core's power and converts it into null-Veyn, an absence of magical energy. It has no worshippers, no theology, no followers. It simply consumes.

In human theology, the World Eater is the ultimate evil — the force that will end the world if not stopped. Temples of the World Core teach that every act of creation weakens the World Eater by reinforcing the Core's dream.

In angel theology, the World Eater is a test — the Core allows it to exist because it forces the faithful to prove their devotion. The angels who guard the realm borders are, in angel theology, defending the Core's dream against the Eater's hunger.

In demon theology, the World Eater is the only honest force in the world — it takes what it wants without pretending to be righteous. Some heretical demon sects secretly admire the World Eater.

5. THE ABYSSAL WYRM — The Sealed Terror

The Abyssal Wyrm predates the division of the three realms. It is not a god, but it is ancient enough to qualify as a primordial force. Sealed beneath the world's crust by the Aelthar, its breath nullifies all Veyn in its path — creating zones of absolute magic silence.

In human theology, the Wyrm is a punishment — the Core's wrath made flesh, sealed away because it destroyed too much. Releasing it would be the end of everything.

In angel theology, the Wyrm is a forgotten sin — something the Aelthar created or attracted through their hubris, then locked away rather than destroy. The angels believe the Wyrm will be released when the Sundering is completed.

In demon theology, the Wyrm is the ultimate weapon — if freed, it could be directed at the Angel Realm. Some demon generals have secretly searched for ways to break the seal.

---

RACE-SPECIFIC RELATIONSHIPS TO THE DIVINE

HUMANS:
  • Primary Religion: World Core Faith (The Dreamer interpretation)
  • Worship Style: Meditation at temples, creation as prayer, offerings of crafted goods
  • Priesthood: None formal — anyone can lead a gathering. The Seer is the closest thing to a high priest.
  • Afterlife Belief: Uncertain. Most humans believe the Core "recycles" their Veyn into new life. Some believe in a peaceful continuation. Some believe in nothing.
  • Sacred Texts: None — the Faith is oral tradition, passed down through meditation practice
  • Religious Conflict: Humans are tolerant of other beliefs because the Faith is non-dogmatic. The only hard line: the World Eater must be stopped.

ANGELS:
  • Primary Religion: Angel Vow Theology (The Arbiter interpretation)
  • Worship Style: Vow Meditation — daily silent reflection on one's promise. Pilgrimage to the Cathedral of the First Vow.
  • Priesthood: The Serapharch is the highest theological authority. The Fifth Pillar (Thalor Elwin) is the Keeper of the Sundering Altar and the Vow's guardian.
  • Afterlife Belief: Angels have no soul — the Vow makes them a spiritual body, a holy form that takes the place of a soul. A well-kept Vow is said to return cleanly to the world core when the angel dies, the promise joining the silent will that holds the world; a broken Vow simply unravels, and with it goes everything the angel was.
  • Sacred Texts: The Vow Scripture — the original incantation spoken at the Sundering Altar, written in angel script
  • Religious Conflict: Angels view demon theology as blasphemy. They view human faith as well-intentioned but naive. They view the Hidden Realm's inhabitants as spiritual orphans.

DEMONS:
  • Primary Religion: None official (The Fuel interpretation)
  • Worship Style: No worship. Strength is the only virtue. The strong take; the weak are taken.
  • Priesthood: None. The Mordrach is the closest thing to a spiritual authority, but only because they are the strongest.
  • Afterlife Belief: Death is final. Veyn returns to the Core. Nothing persists. This makes demons fearless and nihilistic.
  • Sacred Texts: None. Demons consider written records a waste of time.
  • Religious Conflict: Demons view angel theology as a chain — the Vow is a leash, not a blessing. They view human faith as cowardice — praying to something that cannot hear you.
  • Heretical Sects: A small minority of demons question the official theology. They point to the Cindergrave Wraiths as proof that death is not always final. These sects are persecuted by the mainstream.

HIDDEN REALM INHABITANTS:
  • Primary Religion: Pragmatism (survival takes precedence over theology)
  • Belief: The Hidden Realm is the Aelthar's original garden — the true home that was stolen. Some inhabitants worship the Aelthar as ancestral spirits. Most just want to survive.
  • Kael von Ashen: The last Aelthar. He does not worship the Core — he was shaped by it. He views the Core as a parent views a child: with love, frustration, and the knowledge that the child must find its own path.

HUMANS (alternative sects):
  • The Seer's Order: Treats the Truthstone as a divine artifact — a fragment of the Core itself. The Seer is the Core's voice. This is the closest thing to organized religion in the Human Realm.
  • The Iron Covenant: Militant humans who reject the Faith's non-violent theology. They believe the Core is weak and that humanity must protect itself through strength, not prayer.
  • The Veil Seekers: Scholars who believe the Aelthar's knowledge is sacred — that recovering it is the highest form of worship.

---

THEOLOGICAL CONFLICTS (story drivers)

1. The Vow vs. The Pact: Angels believe promises should be binding through divine authority. Demons believe contracts should be binding through mutual self-interest. Humans try to find a middle ground through the Broker's Guild. This is not just philosophy — it shapes how every treaty, marriage, and alliance is structured.

2. The Dreamer vs. The Fuel: Is the World Core a god that deserves worship, or a resource to be exploited? This question divides every council, every battlefield, every Academy classroom.

3. The Wraith Problem: If death is final (demon theology), why do Cindergrave Wraiths exist? If death leads to peace (angel theology), why do the Echoes of the Fallen still fight? The existence of spirits challenges every religion's claims about the afterlife.

4. The Hybrid's Theological Crisis: Jaiden Marlock cannot take the Vow (no single promise binds both natures) and cannot reject it (his angel half requires it). He exists outside every theology — proof that the world's religious categories are incomplete.

5. The World Eater's Silence: If the Core is conscious (angel/human view), why doesn't it fight the World Eater? If the Core is just a resource (demon view), then the Eater is simply a better predator. Either answer is terrifying.

---

SACRED PRACTICES BY RACE

Humans:
  • Meditation (World Core Faith) — sitting in silence, connecting to the Core
  • Creation offerings — crafted goods left at temples
  • The Seer's Vigil — when a Healer dies, the Seer enters solitary meditation with the Truthstone
  • Festival of the Dead — honoring those whose Veyn has returned to the Core

Angels:
  • Vow Meditation — daily silent reflection on one's promise
  • Vow Renewal — annual ceremony at the Cathedral of the First Vow
  • Promise Chains — public declarations of intent, witnessed by the community
  • The Echo Ceremony — when an angel dies, their final words are recorded and stored in the Memory Libraries

Demons:
  • The Pit Challenge — the closest thing to religious ritual; proving strength through combat
  • Blood Tithe — offering blood to the Obsidian Spires (not worship, but tradition)
  • The Arena Games — gladiatorial combat that serves as both entertainment and social ritual
  • Remembrance of the Fallen — demons who died are acknowledged, not honored

Hidden Realm:
  • Communal Fire — gathering around fire for warmth, storytelling, and survival
  • The Wanderer's Bargain — treating the Wanderer's appearances as spiritual events
  • Aelthar Remembrance — some inhabitants leave offerings at Aelthar ruins

name: The Exorcist Rites
subtitle: Sacred ceremonies of purification and banishment
description:
The Exorcist class maintains a set of sacred rites that blend combat technique with spiritual practice. These rites are the closest thing the Half-Made World has to organized religious ceremony.

The Rite of Purification is the most common — used to cleanse corrupted Veyn from a person, place, or object. The Exorcist channels holy energy through specific incantations and gestures, burning away corruption while leaving the uncorrupted Veyn intact. This is the primary treatment for Corruption Sickness in its early stages.

The Rite of Expulsion is used against spirits and undead. The Exorcist identifies the spiritual anchor binding the spirit to the physical world and severs it, releasing the spirit into whatever afterlife the world provides. This is the only reliable way to permanently destroy Ashbound Spirits, Gloomveil Specters, and other spirit-class entities.

The Rite of Sealing is the most powerful and dangerous — used to bind entities that cannot be destroyed. The Exorcist creates a Veyn seal that contains the target within a defined space. This is how Vireth was sealed in the Sentient River, though the rite required multiple high-rank Exorcists working together.

The Rite of Restoration is the gentlest — used to heal spiritual damage, vow-scarring, and the aftermath of Vow breaking. It cannot reverse a broken Vow, but it can ease the physical and spiritual pain that follows.

name: Angel Vow Theology
subtitle: How angels understand their spiritual covenant
description:
Angels do not follow the World Core Faith — they have their own theological framework centered on the Vow.

Angels believe the Vow is not just a contract but a spiritual covenant with the world itself. When an angel speaks the incantation at the Sundering Altar, they are not making a promise to a ruler or a god — they are making a promise to existence. The halo is the physical proof that the world accepted their promise.

This theology teaches that the world core is not dormant but discerning — it watches every Vow, every promise, every oath, and it rewards those who keep their word with steady Veyn and bright halos. Those who break their word lose the world's trust, and their halo shatters.

Angels do not pray in the human sense. Instead, they practice 'Vow Meditation' — sitting in silence and reflecting on their promise, reinforcing their commitment through introspection. This practice is considered sacred and is performed daily by devout angels.

The highest theological concept in angel theology is 'The Unbroken Chain' — the idea that every angel's Vow connects to every other angel's Vow through the world core, creating a web of promises that holds reality together. Breaking one Vow weakens the entire chain, which is why Fallen Angels are treated with such severity — they have damaged the fabric of reality itself.

name: Demon Afterlife Beliefs
subtitle: What demons believe happens after death
description:
Demons have a grim view of the afterlife. Unlike humans who hope for peace, demons believe that death is final — there is nothing beyond it.

Demon theology teaches that Veyn is borrowed, not owned. When a demon dies, their Veyn returns to the world core and is redistributed to the living. There is no soul, no spirit, no continuation. The demon simply ceases to exist, and their Veyn feeds the next generation.

This belief makes demons both fearless and nihilistic. They fight without hesitation because they believe death is the natural end of all things. They breed recklessly because they believe the dead will be replaced by the living. They conquer without remorse because they believe the strong deserve to live and the weak deserve to be consumed.

The exception to this is the Cindergrave Wraiths — demons who died in Lethmoor's fall and whose wills persisted as spirits. To mainstream demon theology, this is an aberration — dead things should not linger. The existence of wraiths suggests that death is not as final as demons believe, which is deeply unsettling to their worldview.

Some heretical demon sects have begun to question the official theology, suggesting that consciousness persists after death in some form. These sects are persecuted by the mainstream demon establishment.

name: The Seer's Prophecy
subtitle: The sacred duty of predicting the next Healer
description:
The Seer's role is considered sacred across the Human Realm, blending religious duty with practical necessity. The Seer is not a priest — they are a Diviner who has been entrusted with the Truthstone, and their predictions are treated as divine revelations.

The process works like this: when a Healer dies, the Seer takes the Truthstone to a quiet place and enters a deep meditative state. The Truthstone glows in response to the Veyn signature of the next Healer — a unique pattern that no two people share. The Seer follows the glow like a compass, eventually locating the individual.

The Seer's predictions are always accurate — the Truthstone has never been wrong. But the process is slow and dangerous. The Seer must travel to wherever the Truthstone leads, often through dangerous territory. They must protect the Truthstone at all costs — if it falls into the wrong hands, the entire Healer succession system collapses.

The Seer's Order maintains that there is only one Truthstone and one Seer at any time. When the current Seer dies, the Truthstone reveals the next Seer to the surviving Guardians. This chain has never been broken in recorded history.

Some believe the Truthstone is a fragment of the world core itself — a piece of the dreaming entity that can sense the Veyn patterns of those destined to serve as healers. If this is true, the Seer's role is not just sacred — it is a direct communication channel with the world core.

name: Temples & Sacred Sites
subtitle: The holy places of the Half-Made World
description:
Several locations across the Half-Made World are considered sacred, drawing worshippers and pilgrims from all three realms.

The Common Altar Temple is the most widely visited sacred site. Located in the neutral zone between the three realms, it houses the Common Sundering Altar where most ordinary people undergo their awakening. The temple is simple — a circular stone structure with the Altar at its center, surrounded by meditation alcoves. Pilgrims come to meditate near the Altar, believing its proximity to the world core amplifies prayer.

The Ether Forest Boundary is considered sacred by the World Core Faith. The point where the Arubian Forest meets the Umbrage Forest — light meeting dark — is believed to be a direct manifestation of the world core's duality. Followers gather there during equinoxes to meditate on balance.

The Angel Realm's Cathedral of the First Vow is where the first angel spoke the Vow to the world core. It is a towering structure of white stone and golden light, with the original Vow carved into its walls in angel script. Angels make pilgrimages here to reaffirm their vows.

The Demon Realm's Obsidian Pit is a deep crater where the first demon supposedly tore its own Veyn channels to gain power. It is a place of dark pilgrimage — demons go there to prove their strength by descending into the pit and surviving its corrupted atmosphere.

The Hidden Realm's Lethmoor Kingdom ruins are sacred to no one, but they draw treasure hunters and scholars who believe the replicated kingdom holds fragments of Aelthar knowledge.

name: Healing Hierarchy
subtitle: The different tiers of medical care in the world
description:
Medical care in the Half-Made World operates on a tiered system based on who provides it.

Tier 1 — Self-Care: Common people treat minor ailments with herbal remedies, poultices, and rest. Herbalists sell basic treatments at market stalls for a few Copper Shards. These work for colds, minor cuts, and stomach ailments but are useless against anything serious.

Tier 2 — Apothecary: Trained herbalists and alchemical assistants who can brew Healing Potions (5-10 Silver Marks) and treat moderate injuries. Apothecaries exist in every town and are the primary medical resource for most people. They cannot treat Corruption Sickness or Veyn-related injuries.

Tier 3 — Clergy Healing: The seven Healers of the Human Realm, holders of the Clergy class. They can heal serious injuries, cure diseases, and reverse early-stage Corruption Sickness. A Clergy healing session costs 2-5 Gold Crowns and requires an appointment. Most people never see a Healer in their lifetime.

Tier 4 — Saintess Healing: Saintesses channel Holy Energy to heal. They are rarer than Clergy and their healing is more powerful, capable of curing conditions that Clergy cannot. A Saintess healing costs 10+ Gold Crowns.

Tier 5 — Angelic Healing: High-rank angels can heal through their Angelic Aura. Only Aetherblade Lord and Serapharch ranks have healing potent enough to matter. This tier is reserved for the ruling class and military emergencies.

name: Herbalism & Apothecaries
subtitle: Non-magical medicine and the shops that provide it
description:
Herbalism is the oldest form of medicine in the Half-Made World, predating magical healing by millennia. Even today, most people rely on herbal remedies for everyday ailments.

Apothecary shops are found in every town, identifiable by the bundle of dried herbs hanging above the door. Inside, rows of labeled jars line the walls, containing everything from common willow bark (for headaches) to rare Aelthar Root (for Veyn fatigue). The apothecary pharmacist mixes remedies on the spot, combining herbs with Veyn-infused water for basic potions.

Common remedies include: Willow Bark Tea (headache, fever), Thornmoss Paste (wound sealing), Ebon Leaf Poultice (infection), and Sunpetal Drops (eye irritation). These cost 1-5 Copper Shards and work reliably for what they treat.

More serious remedies require rare ingredients: Dragon Scale Powder (bone healing), Skywhale Blubber Salve (burns), and Pixie Dust Infusion (permanent Veyn boost). These are expensive — 10+ Gold Crowns — and only available in major cities.

The apothecary trade is regulated by local authorities. Pharmacists must pass a knowledge test to operate, and selling counterfeit remedies is punished with public flogging and permanent ban from the trade.

name: Diseases & Epidemics
subtitle: The illnesses that plague the Half-Made World
description:
The Half-Made World has several diseases that affect its inhabitants, some mundane and some magical.

Mundane Diseases: Common cold, fever, infection, and intestinal parasites are treated by herbalists and apothecaries. More serious are lungrot (a respiratory disease common in mining towns), blood-fever (a contagious hemorrhagic illness that sweeps through crowded cities), and bone-wasting (a degenerative condition that weakens the skeleton over years).

Magical Diseases: Corruption Sickness (corrupted Veyn exposure), Saturation Sickness (concentrated Veyn exposure), and Vow Decay (spiritual deterioration from breaking promises) are all treated differently and require magical intervention.

Plagues: The most devastating plague in recorded history was the Miasma Plague, which swept through the Demon Realm three centuries ago. Corrupted Veyn leaked from the Umbrage Forest and infected thousands. The plague killed more demons in a single year than any war — and it was only contained when a group of Exorcists performed a mass Purification Rite at the forest's edge.

Epidemics are treated by Clergy Healers when possible, but the seven Healers cannot be everywhere. Towns without Healer access rely on quarantine — isolating the sick in designated buildings until the disease burns through the population or herbalists find a treatment.

name: Food & Cuisine
subtitle: What people eat across the three realms
description:
Food varies dramatically by realm and social class.

The Human Realm has the most diverse cuisine. Common meals consist of bread (wheat or rye), cheese, stewed meat, root vegetables, and ale. Fish is common near rivers and coasts. The capital city's restaurants serve exotic dishes using ingredients from the Ether Forest — Arubian mushrooms, Fairy-blessed herbs, and forest berries. Fine dining involves multiple courses, imported wines, and dishes prepared by skilled chefs who use basic Veyn to enhance flavors.

The Angel Realm's cuisine is simple and refined. Angels eat light meals — fruits, nuts, honey, and Veyn-infused water that sustains them without heavy food. High-rank angels barely need to eat at all, drawing sustenance directly from ambient Veyn. Lumen civilians eat more substantially but still favor clean, unprocessed foods. Angel cuisine is known for its elegance — small portions, perfect presentation, and the subtle use of Veyn to preserve freshness.

The Demon Realm's cuisine is brutal and utilitarian. Demons eat whatever they can kill — raw meat, roasted beast, fermented blood drinks. Gnash traders who spend time in the Human Realm develop a taste for human food, which they consider a weakness. Demon cuisine is not meant to be enjoyed; it is meant to fuel the body for fighting.

The Hidden Realm has no cuisine — time is slowed so hunger barely registers. Travelers survive on whatever they carry or whatever they can hunt.

name: Clothing & Fashion
subtitle: What people wear across the realms
description:
Clothing reflects realm, class, and function.

Human Realm fashion ranges from simple wool tunics for laborers to elaborate embroidered silk for nobles. Common workers wear practical clothing — linen shirts, leather breeches, sturdy boots. Merchants wear finer fabrics but nothing ostentatious. Nobles wear layered robes of silk and velvet, dyed in rich colors (red, blue, gold) that signify their status. Military wear is standardized — leather armor for Wardens, plate for elite guards.

Angel Realm fashion is elegant and minimal. Angels favor flowing white and gold garments that complement their wings. Lumen wear simple tunics; Virtues wear fitted robes; Aetherblade Lords wear battle-ready attire with armored plates; the Serapharch wears a single golden sash that represents the weight of rule. Angels never wear heavy clothing — it interferes with their wings.

Demon Realm fashion is aggressive and functional. Demons wear dark leather, chain, and bone. Gnash traders wear cloaks to hide their horns and wings under Duskveil. Bloodwards wear crimson-stained armor. Mordrach wear almost nothing — their power is their appearance, and they want nothing to obscure it.

The Wanderer wears a tattered gray cloak that seems to shift and blur at the edges, as though it exists in multiple places at once. No one has ever seen the Wanderer's face.

fields.value: Linen shirts, leather breeches, sturdy boots — practical and plain

fields.label: Human Nobles
fields.value: Layered silk and velvet robes — red, blue, gold signify status

fields.label: Angel Fashion
fields.value: Flowing white and gold — minimal, elegant, never interferes with wings

fields.label: Demon Fashion
fields.value: Dark leather, chain, bone — aggressive and functional

fields.label: The Wanderer
fields.value: Tattered gray cloak that shifts and blurs — face never seen

name: Greetings & Social Customs
subtitle: How people interact across the realms
description:
Social customs vary dramatically by realm and race.

Human Realm greetings are formal and context-dependent. Commoners nod or wave. Merchants clasp hands (a gesture of trust — both hands visible means no weapons). Nobles bow at the waist — the depth of the bow indicates relative status. Between equals, a brief nod suffices. Between a superior and subordinate, the subordinate bows deeply. Physical contact between strangers is avoided — touching someone without permission is considered aggressive.

Angel Realm greetings center on the halo. Angels greet by briefly brightening their halo toward the other person — a gesture of acknowledgment and respect. The brightness indicates the sincerity of the greeting. A dim halo flick is dismissive; a bright one is warm. Between close friends, angels may touch foreheads — sharing the light of their halos.

Demon Realm greetings are territorial. Demons acknowledge each other by scent — sniffing the air near the other person. This identifies rank, health, and intent. Physical greetings between demons involve clashing fists — a test of strength disguised as a handshake. Weak demons are expected to submit (lower their head) when greeting a stronger demon.

Cross-realm customs: When interacting with someone from another realm, the standard practice is to mirror their greeting style. A human meeting an angel will bow; an angel meeting a demon will maintain distance. Ignoring these customs is considered rude but not hostile.

fields.label: Human Formal
fields.value: Nod (equals), bow (superior), hand-clasp (merchants) — physical contact avoided

fields.label: Angel Halo Greeting
fields.value: Brightening halo toward the other — brightness indicates sincerity

fields.label: Angel Forehead Touch
fields.value: Between close friends — sharing the light of their halos

fields.label: Demon Scent Greeting
fields.value: Sniffing the air — identifies rank, health, and intent

fields.label: Demon Fist Clash
fields.value: Clashing fists — test of strength disguised as handshake

fields.label: Cross-Realm
fields.value: Mirror the other's greeting style — ignoring is rude but not hostile

name: Taboos & Prohibitions
subtitle: The things that are forbidden or deeply offensive
description:
Every realm has taboos that go beyond written law — breaking them invites social ostracism, not just punishment.

Universal Taboos: Killing a Lightwisp darkens the ambient Veyn for hours and is universally considered wrong. Harming a Dreamweaver causes Veyn darkening for weeks. Killing a Stonehollow Elk is deeply taboo among Pallantine Elves and guaranteed to bring forest retaliation. Touching someone's halo (for angels) or horns (for demons) without permission is a grave insult.

Human Realm Taboos: Breaking a promise is socially devastating — humans cannot recover reputation easily. Speaking ill of the Healers is considered blasphemous. Entering the Ether Forest without proper preparation is seen as suicidal stupidity, not bravery.

Angel Realm Taboos: Questioning someone's Vow is deeply offensive — it implies they might break their word. Wearing black (the color of Fallen Angels) in public is avoided. Mentioning the Six Pillars' deaths in casual conversation is forbidden.

Demon Realm Taboos: Showing weakness in public is dangerous — it invites challenges. Refusing a combat challenge without cause is cowardice. Hoarding food when others are hungry is considered a Mordrach-level offense.

fields.label: Lightwisp Harm
fields.value: Darkens ambient Veyn — universally wrong

fields.label: Dreamweaver Harm
fields.value: Causes Veyn darkening for weeks — deeply taboo

fields.label: Stonehollow Elk Kill
fields.value: Taboo among Pallantine — brings forest retaliation

fields.label: Angel Halo Touch
fields.value: Grave insult — never touch without permission

fields.label: Demon Weakness
fields.value: Showing weakness in public invites challenges

fields.label: Vow Questioning
fields.value: Implies someone might break their word — deeply offensive to angels

name: Funeral Customs
subtitle: How the dead are honored across realms
description:
Death customs reflect each realm's beliefs about the afterlife.

Human Realm funerals are communal events. The body is washed, dressed in white (the color of peace), and placed on a stone bier. Family members place personal items around the body — tools of the deceased's trade, favorite foods, letters. The body is then burned on a funeral pyre, and the ashes are scattered in the nearest body of water. The belief is that water carries the Veyn back to the world core. A feast follows, where stories of the deceased are shared.

Angel Realm funerals are silent and luminous. The angel's body is placed in a circle of lightwax candles, and surrounding angels dim their halos in mourning. The body is not burned — it is left to dissolve into pure Veyn over several days, returning to the ambient energy pool. The most powerful angels may leave behind a 'Veyn Echo' — a lingering presence that can be felt by other angels for years.

Demon Realm funerals are violent celebrations. When a demon dies, their war-band holds a 'Death Feast' — a chaotic event involving fighting, drinking, and the ritual consumption of the dead demon's heart. This is not desecration; it is considered the highest honor, transferring the dead demon's strength to the living. The stronger the demon who eats the heart, the greater the honor.

When an angel becomes a Fallen Angel, there is no funeral — they are simply cast out. The community mourns the loss of a Vow-keeper but does not acknowledge the Fallen as dead.

fields.label: Human Funeral
fields.value: White-clad body, personal items, funeral pyre, ashes scattered in water

fields.label: Angel Funeral
fields.value: Silent and luminous — body dissolves into Veyn over days, may leave Veyn Echo

fields.label: Demon Death Feast
fields.value: Violent celebration — war-band eats the dead demon's heart for strength

fields.label: Fallen Angel
fields.value: No funeral — cast out; community mourns the lost Vow-keeper

name: Graveyards & Memorials
subtitle: Where the dead are remembered
description:
Memorial practices vary by race and realm.

Human Realm graveyards are common in towns and cities. Graves are marked with simple stone headstones engraved with the deceased's name, date of death, and a brief epitaph. Wealthy families build mausoleums. The largest memorial in the Human Realm is the Wall of Names in the capital — a massive stone wall inscribed with every human who died in the Miasma Plague. New names are added annually on the Shatter Remembrance day.

Angel Realm memorials are trees — specifically, Everlight Trees, a species found only in the angel realm that glows with perpetual golden light. When an angel dies, a seed is planted in their memory. The tree grows for centuries, serving as a living memorial. The oldest Everlight Trees are over ten thousand years old and are considered sacred.

The Demon Realm has no graveyards or memorials. Dead demons are consumed (heart eaten) or left to rot. There are no headstones, no markers, no remembrance. The only exception is the Obsidian Pillar — a monolith in the Demon Realm capital where the names of fallen Bloodward-rank demons are carved. Lower ranks are not remembered.

The Aelthar battlefield is its own memorial — the Echoes of the Fallen still fight there, making it a living memorial to the war that destroyed them.

fields.label: Human Graveyards
fields.value: Stone headstones, mausoleums for wealthy; Wall of Names memorial for plague victims

fields.label: Angel Everlight Trees
fields.value: Golden-glowing trees planted for each dead angel — some 10,000+ years old

fields.label: Demon Remembrance
fields.value: None — dead consumed or left to rot; only Bloodward names carved on Obsidian Pillar

fields.label: Aelthar Battlefield
fields.value: Living memorial — Echoes still fight, honoring the war that destroyed them

name: Marriage Customs
subtitle: How unions work across the realms
description:
Marriage is practiced differently by each race.

Human Realm marriage is a legal contract witnessed by a Magistrate. The couple exchanges vows and a token (usually a ring or pendant) in front of family and witnesses. The Magistrate seals the contract with a Veyn signature — a small, permanent mark on the marriage certificate that proves its authenticity. Divorce is possible but socially devastating and legally expensive. Most marriages are arranged by families for economic or political advantage, though love marriages are becoming more common in cities.

Angel Realm marriage is a Vow merging. Two angels speak their individual Vows simultaneously, and the world core binds them together. The result is a shared Vow that links their halos — they glow brighter when together and dimmer when apart. This bond is permanent and cannot be broken without both becoming Fallen Angels. Angels marry once and for eternity.

Demon Realm marriage does not exist. Demons form temporary alliances through combat and breeding agreements, but these are not recognized as formal unions. Gnash demons sometimes sign contracts with humans that mimic marriage, but these are financial arrangements, not romantic ones.

Hybrid marriages (human-angel, human-demon) are rare and controversial. The Academy facilitates these when they occur, but both families face social pressure.

fields.label: Human Marriage
fields.value: Legal contract witnessed by Magistrate — Veyn-sealed certificate; divorce possible but devastating

fields.label: Angel Vow Merging
fields.value: Two angels speak Vows simultaneously — halos link permanently; breaking = both become Fallen

fields.label: Demon Unions
fields.value: No formal marriage — temporary alliances through combat and breeding agreements

fields.label: Hybrid Marriages
fields.value: Rare and controversial — Academy facilitates but families face social pressure

name: Family Structure
subtitle: How families are organized in each realm
description:
Family structure varies by race and class.

Human families follow a patriarchal or matriarchal structure depending on the region. In the capital, the eldest parent holds authority; in rural areas, the father typically leads. Extended families often live together — grandparents, parents, children, and aunts/uncles sharing a single compound. Inheritance passes to the eldest child, though a Magistrate can override this in cases of disinheritance.

Angel families are small — angels barely breed and each child is a significant event. Angels raise children collectively; the concept of a 'nuclear family' doesn't exist. A young angel is cared for by the community, with multiple adults sharing responsibility. When an angel comes of age (at 15), the community gathers at the Sundering Altar for the Vow ceremony.

Demon families are structured around power, not blood. A demon 'family' is a war-band led by the strongest individual. Breeding is a duty, not a relationship — Mordrach produce offspring to maintain the ranks, not out of affection. Gnash demons who live in the Human Realm sometimes adopt human family structures as part of their Duskveil disguise.

The concept of 'chosen family' is common across all realms — fighters who battle together often form bonds stronger than blood. Military units, Academy classmates, and Broker partnerships all create surrogate families.

fields.label: Human Extended Families
fields.value: Grandparents, parents, children, aunts/uncles — often share a compound

fields.label: Angel Collective Raising
fields.value: Children cared for by community — multiple adults share responsibility

fields.label: Demon War-Band Family
fields.value: Power-based, not blood-based — breeding is duty, not relationship

fields.label: Chosen Family
fields.value: Bonds from fighting together — stronger than blood across all realms

name: Human Class Hierarchy
subtitle: The five tiers of Human society
description:
Human society is divided into five tiers, each defined by power, knowledge, wealth, labor, or exile. Movement between tiers is possible but rare — it requires either birth, Academy admission, extraordinary wealth, or a fall from grace.

Crown: Ruby Divina and her immediate family, plus the high-ranking officials she appoints — magistrates, senior military officers, and trusted advisors. They live in the capital's palace district, eat the finest food, wear silk and gold, and make decisions that affect millions. Moving into Crown requires either birth or extraordinary achievement recognized by the ruler.

Inscribed: Academy-trained professionals with Veyn sensitivity — healers, enchanters, scholars, and researchers. They carry the Academy's mark and hold social prestige that rivals Crown in intellectual circles. They live in comfortable quarters near Academy branches, earn well, and are exempt from most labor taxes. Moving from Dustborn to Inscribed requires Academy admission, which demands Veyn sensitivity that most Dustborn lack.

Bartered: Wealthy merchants, guild masters, and successful traders. They live comfortably in the merchant quarters, eat well, and wear fine clothes. They have more gold than most Crown officials but less political power. Some Bartered buy their way into minor noble titles. They are defined by the contracts they hold and the deals they make — the Broker's Guild enforces their agreements.

Dustborn: Laborers, farmers, servants, craftsmen, and unskilled workers. They live day-to-day, earning 1-2 Silver Marks per day. They eat simple food, wear practical clothing, and have little savings. Most humans are Dustborn — they are the backbone of the economy, the hands that build and harvest. Their name comes from the dust of the fields and workshops.

Shorn: Criminals, exiles, and those without realm affiliation. They have been cut from society — no legal protection, no guild membership, no social standing. They survive on the margins, begging, scavenging, or working illegal jobs. Being Shorn is a permanent mark; even if a Shorn person reforms, society rarely accepts them back.

fields.value: Ruby Divina and officials — palace district, silk and gold, political power

fields.label: Inscribed
fields.value: Academy-trained Veyn users — scholars, healers, enchanters, social prestige

fields.value: Merchants and guild masters — wealth through trade, contracts enforced by Broker's Guild

name: Angel Class Hierarchy
subtitle: The social strata of the Angel Realm
description:
Angel society is defined by rank, but rank does not equal class.

The Serapharch: Clint Ashborn and the ruling position. Absolute authority over the Angel Realm. Lives in the Cathedral of the First Vow. The Serapharch's word is law.

The Six Pillars: The six Aetherblade Lord Angels who serve as the highest military and political officers. They are the closest thing angels have to a noble class. Each Pillar commands a section of the Angel Army and oversees a district of the Angel Realm.

The Noble Tier: High-ranking Aetherblade Lords and senior Virtues who hold political or military positions. They live in the upper districts of angel cities, with larger homes and more Veyn-rich environments.

The Common Tier: Lumen and lower Virtues who work as civilians — craftsmen, merchants, farmers, scholars. They live in the lower districts. Most angels are Lumen, and most Lumen live quiet, ordinary lives.

The Fallen: Cast-out angels with broken halos. They have no class, no standing, and no community. They survive in the Human Realm behind Dawnveil, hiding their true nature.

fields.label: Serapharch
fields.value: Absolute authority — Clint Ashborn, word is law

fields.label: Six Pillars
fields.value: Six Aetherblade Lords — military/political officers, district commanders

name: Demon Class Hierarchy
subtitle: The social strata of the Demon Realm
description:
Demon society is the most brutal and straightforward — power determines everything.

The Mordrach: Tera Morage and the ruling position. Absolute authority. A Mordrach can kill any demon below them without consequence. The Mordrach's word is the only law.

The Bloodward Elite: Bloodward-rank demons who serve as military commanders, city governors, and the Mordrach's inner circle. They enforce the Mordrach's will and maintain order through fear and strength.

The Scourge Warriors: Mid-rank demons who form the backbone of the demon army. They are soldiers, laborers, and fighters. Most demons are Scourge.

The Gnash Underclass: The lowest rank. Gnash are laborers, traders, and the most expendable members of demon society. They can make contracts with anyone — a ability that gives them economic value but also makes them targets. Many Gnash flee to the Human Realm behind Duskveil.

The Nameless: Demons who have lost their rank through failure or cowardice. They are stripped of their name and forced to live as scavengers. Being Nameless is worse than death in demon culture.

fields.value: Tera Morage — absolute authority; can kill any lesser demon without consequence

fields.label: Bloodward Elite
fields.value: Military commanders and governors — enforce Mordrach's will through fear

name: Seasons & Weather
subtitle: How the world's climate changes through the year
description:
The Half-Made World has four distinct seasons, each affecting the realms differently.

Spring (Bloom Month — Verdant Month): The Arubian Forest explodes with life. Fairies are most active, and the Pallantine Elves hold their annual Blessing of the Trees ceremony. In the Demon Realm, new monster spawns peak — Trolls and Orcs breed aggressively. The Hidden Realm portal is weakest during spring, as ambient Veyn is dispersed by new growth.

Summer (Glow Month — Veil Month): The hottest season across all realms. The Umbrage Forest's darker areas become nearly impassable as heat and corrupted Veyn combine to create 'Miasma Fog' — a dangerous haze that causes Corruption Sickness in unprotected humans. Angels celebrate the Glow Festival. The Ether Forest boundary thinnest during Veil Month.

Autumn (Shatter Month — Dusk Month): Harvest season in the Human Realm. The Shatter Remembrance observance dominates the middle of autumn. In the Demon Realm, the weakened and injured from summer battles die off, reducing the population before winter. The Hidden Realm's time-slowed environment means seasons barely affect it.

Winter (Frost Month — Awakening Month): The coldest and most dangerous season. Travel between realms becomes hazardous as roads ice over and monsters grow desperate for food. The Sundering Altar ceremonies happen at the tail end of winter — children who turned 15 during the year undergo awakening as winter ends and spring begins.

fields.value: Forest blooms, monster spawns peak, portal weakest, Elf Blessing ceremony

fields.label: Summer
fields.value: Miasma Fog in Umbrage Forest, Glow Festival, Ether Forest boundary thinnest

fields.label: Autumn
