name: Natural Disasters
subtitle: The catastrophes that threaten the world
description:
The Half-Made World faces several recurring natural disasters, some mundane and some magical.

Veyn Storms: When ambient Veyn concentration spikes in an area, it can erupt into a Veyn Storm — a chaotic tempest of raw magical energy that scrambles spells, disrupts enchantments, and can cause Saturation Sickness in anyone caught in it. Veyn Storms are unpredictable and can last hours or days. They are most common near the Ether Forest and the Hidden Realm portal.

Miasma Eruptions: When corrupted Veyn from the Umbrage Forest leaks across the border, it creates a Miasma Eruption — a wave of dark energy that sickens humans and animals. Exorcists are deployed to contain these eruptions, but in severe cases, entire villages must be evacuated.

Earthquakes: The world's Veyn channels shift periodically, causing earthquakes. The most violent earthquakes occur near the Hidden Realm, where the unstable Veyn terrain creates fault lines. Lethmoor Kingdom sits on one of the most seismically active zones.

Dragon Rampages: When a Dragon's territory is invaded or its nest threatened, the resulting rampage can destroy entire settlements. Dragon Rampages are classified as natural disasters because they cannot be prevented — only survived.

World Core Tremors: Rare but terrifying. When the World Eater drains a particularly large amount of Veyn from the core, the world itself shudders. Buildings crack, Veyn channels destabilize, and every fighter in the world feels a momentary dip in their power. World Core Tremors happen once every few centuries and are considered omens of catastrophe.

fields.label: Miasma Eruptions
fields.value: Corrupted Veyn leaks from Umbrage — sickens humans, requires Exorcist containment

fields.value: Veyn channel shifts — most violent near Hidden Realm fault lines

name: Flora & Fauna Catalog
subtitle: Plants and animals unique to each realm
description:
Each realm has unique flora and fauna shaped by its Veyn environment.

Human Realm: Common crops (wheat, barley, potatoes), domesticated animals (horses, cattle, chickens), and Ether Forest edge creatures (Fairies, Pallantine wildlife). The Arubian Forest is rich with Veyn-infused plants — Sunpetal flowers that glow at night, Thornmoss that seals wounds, and Everbloom vines that never die.

Angel Realm: Everlight Trees (golden-glowing memorial trees), Angelic Orchids (flowers that only bloom near high concentrations of Holy Energy), and Harmonic Birds (small songbirds whose calls stabilize ambient Veyn). Angels keep domesticated creatures similar to humans but with longer lifespans.

Demon Realm: Corruption-resistant plants (Blackthorn, Ironvine), predatory flora (Strangler Root, Bite Blossom), and aggressive fauna (blood-drinking insects, shadow cats). The Umbrage Forest's ecosystem is hostile to non-demons — everything there has evolved to survive in corrupted Veyn.

Hidden Realm: Time-distorted organisms — plants that grow decades in what feels like days (due to time dilation), creatures that exist in multiple time states simultaneously, and the Ebonspire Tree (100-year-old tree that grows near dragon nests).

Ether Forest: The boundary zone contains hybrid organisms — creatures and plants that exhibit both Arubian (light) and Umbrage (dark) characteristics. These hybrids are rare and valuable to Alchemists.

fields.value: Common crops, domesticated animals, Arubian edge flora (Sunpetal, Thornmoss, Everbloom)

fields.value: Everlight Trees, Angelic Orchids, Harmonic Birds — Veyn-stabilizing ecosystem

fields.label: Demon Realm
fields.value: Hostile to non-demons — Blackthorn, Strangler Root, blood-drinking insects

name: Veyn Density Zones
subtitle: Where magic is strong and where it is weak
description:
Veyn density varies dramatically across the world, creating zones of magical strength and weakness.

High-Density Zones: Areas where Veyn concentration is extremely high. These include the Ether Forest (especially the boundary), areas near the Sundering Altar, and regions close to the Hidden Realm portal. Fighters in high-density zones are significantly stronger — Mages can cast more powerful spells, Alchemists brew better potions, and healers work faster. The downside is Saturation Sickness for those who stay too long.

Low-Density Zones: Areas where Veyn has been depleted or was never concentrated. The desert regions at the edges of the Human Realm, the deep ocean, and the void between realms are all low-density. Fighters here are weaker — spells cost more, healing is slower, and Veyn-based abilities function at reduced capacity.

Corrupted Zones: Areas saturated with corrupted Veyn. The Umbrage Forest is the largest corrupted zone, but smaller pockets exist wherever demons have settled or Miasma Eruptions have occurred. Humans in corrupted zones risk Corruption Sickness; angels risk Vow destabilization.

Null Zones: The rarest and most dangerous — areas where all Veyn has been completely drained. Only the Abyssal Wyrm's breath creates true null zones. In a null zone, no magic functions at all — no Veyn, no Ren, no Holy Energy. Fighters are reduced to their raw physical capabilities. Only world-core material weapons (Shudon-grade metal) remain effective.

fields.value: Ether Forest, Altar vicinity, portal areas — fighters stronger, Saturation Sickness risk

fields.label: Low-Density Zones

fields.label: Corrupted Zones

name: Languages of the World
subtitle: What people speak across the realms
description:
The Half-Made World has several distinct languages and dialects.

Common Tongue: The trade language spoken across all three realms. It evolved from the ancient Aelthar language and is understood by everyone. The Academy teaches Common Tongue as a requirement for all students regardless of race. Most books, contracts, and official documents are written in Common Tongue.

Angel Script: The written language of the angels — flowing, luminous characters that glow faintly when written by an angel. Angel Script is used for religious texts, Vow inscriptions, and official angel documents. Speaking Angel Script aloud produces harmonic tones that can stabilize ambient Veyn. The Cathedral of the First Vow's walls are inscribed entirely in Angel Script.

Demon Fang: The spoken language of demons — harsh, guttural sounds that sound aggressive even in casual conversation. Demons use Common Tongue for trade but speak Demon Fang among themselves. The language has no written form — demons consider writing a waste of time when you can remember or just take what you need.

Elven Whisper: The language of both Pallantine and Veilborn Elves — a soft, melodic tongue spoken at low volume. Elves can communicate at distances up to a mile using Elven Whisper by modulating their Veyn through the words. The language has two dialects: Pallantine (lighter, more musical) and Veilborn (darker, more clipped).

Aelthar Tongue: The ancient language of the Aelthar — now nearly extinct. Only fragments survive in the Academy's archives and on the Sundering Altar's inscriptions. Speaking Aelthar Tongue aloud produces powerful Veyn resonance effects, which is why the Academy restricts access to surviving texts.

name: Naming Conventions
subtitle: How people are named across the realms
description:
Names carry meaning and cultural weight in the Half-Made World.

Human names follow a First Name + Family Name structure. Common first names are short and strong (Jaiden, Sofia, Marcus, Elena). Family names often reference trades, locations, or ancestors (Marlock = 'sea warrior,' Ashborn = 'born of ash,' Divina = 'divine'). Nobles sometimes add a title prefix (Lord Ashborn, Lady Marlock). Commoners rarely use titles.

Angel names are given at the Vow ceremony, not at birth. The name is chosen by the angel themselves during their Vow meditation — it reflects the truth they choose to carry. Angel names are typically single words that evoke concepts (Clint = 'pure light,' Thalor = 'fifth guardian'). Angels do not have family names; they are identified by rank and name (Serapharch Clint, not Clint Ashborn).

Demon names are earned, not given. A demon receives a birth designation (a number or letter code) and must earn their name through achievement. A Scourge who kills a powerful enemy might be named 'Bloodrender.' A Gnash who completes a difficult contract might be named 'Oathbreaker' (ironic, since demons don't honor contracts the way angels honor Vows). Tera Morage is one of the few demons with a two-part name — 'Morage' means 'eternal hunger' in Demon Fang.

Elven names are flowing and nature-inspired. Pallantine Elves use light-themed names (Aelindra = 'sun daughter,' Faelor = 'forest lord'). Veilborn Elves use shadow-themed names (Umbrath = 'shadow walker,' Nyxari = 'night whisper'). Elves use clan names instead of family names.

fields.label: Human Names
fields.value: First + Family — Marlock, Ashborn; nobles add title prefix

fields.label: Angel Names
fields.value: Self-chosen during Vow ceremony — single words reflecting chosen truth

fields.label: Demon Names
fields.value: Earned through achievement — birth designation replaced by deeds

fields.label: Elven Names

name: Music & Performance
subtitle: What people listen to and watch
description:
Music and performance vary by realm and class.

Human Realm music is rich and diverse. Tavern songs tell stories of heroes and monsters. Court musicians play delicate string compositions for nobles. Street performers play percussion and wind instruments in market squares. The most valued musical tradition is 'Veyn Singing' — a technique where the singer channels Veyn through their voice, creating harmonics that can soothe, strengthen, or even heal listeners. Veyn Singing is practiced by trained musicians and is considered both art and mild magic.

Angel Realm music is entirely vocal — angels do not use instruments. Angel choirs produce layered harmonics that can stabilize Veyn across entire cities. The most sacred angel music is the 'Vow Chant' — a communal singing of the Vow incantation that creates a field of pure, steady Veyn around the singers. Angels consider instrumental music crude.

Demon Realm music is rhythmic and aggressive — war drums, bone flutes, and throat singing. Demons do not perform for entertainment; their music is purely functional, used to coordinate military movements and intimidate enemies. The exception is Gnash traders who have adopted human music as part of their Duskveil disguise.

Theatrical performances exist primarily in the Human Realm. Troupes of actors travel between towns performing morality plays, historical dramas, and comedies. The most popular plays tell stories of the Aelthar and the Sundering, though the details are often dramatized beyond recognition.

fields.value: Channeling Veyn through voice — soothes, strengthens, heals listeners

fields.label: Angel Choirs

fields.label: Demon Music
fields.value: War drums, bone flutes — purely functional for coordination and intimidation

fields.value: Traveling troupes perform morality plays, historical dramas, comedies

name: Games & Recreation
subtitle: What people do for fun
description:
Recreation in the Half-Made World ranges from common games to dangerous sports.

Common Games: Chess-like strategy games (called 'Throne' in the Human Realm — played on a hexagonal board), dice games (popular in taverns), and card games (using a deck of 52 illustrated cards depicting creatures and heroes). These are played across all classes.

Combat Sports: Arena fighting is popular in the Human Realm. Fighters compete in controlled bouts for prize money and reputation. The most famous arena is the Ashwell Colosseum in the capital, where fighters up to D-rank compete. Higher-rank fights are too destructive for enclosed spaces.

Hunting: Angel and Human nobility hunt in the Ether Forest, though Pallantine Rangers restrict how deep they can go. Demon 'hunts' are actually wars — Scourge war-bands hunt monsters for sport and sustenance.

Skyriding: Pallantine Elves ride Griffens in aerial competitions — racing, obstacle courses, and formation flying. Skyriding tournaments are major social events in the Arubian Forest.

Veyn Chess: A magical variant of chess where players channel small amounts of Veyn through their pieces, creating subtle effects on the board. Popular among Academy students and noble houses.

fields.label: Throne
fields.value: Hexagonal strategy game — the chess equivalent of the Half-Made World

fields.label: Dice & Card Games
fields.value: Tavern staples — dice for gambling, 52-card illustrated decks

fields.label: Arena Fighting
fields.value: Controlled combat bouts — Ashwell Colosseum is the most famous venue

fields.label: Skyriding
fields.value: Pallantine Griffen racing — major social tournaments in the Arubian Forest

fields.label: Veyn Chess
fields.value: Magical chess variant — pieces channel Veyn; popular at Academy and noble houses

name: Spy Networks
subtitle: How realms gather information on each other
description:
Every realm maintains intelligence networks, though their methods differ.

The Human Realm has the 'Crown Eyes' — a network of spies operating under Ruby Divina's direct authority. Crown Eyes agents are Veilrunners who have been recruited and trained specifically for espionage. They operate in all three realms, gathering information on military movements, political alliances, and potential threats. The network's greatest asset is its anonymity — no one knows who is and isn't a Crown Eye.

The Angel Realm uses Lumen as its intelligence network. Because Lumen look ordinary and are considered unimportant, they can move through any realm without suspicion. An angel Lumen working as a shopkeeper in the Human Realm might actually be reporting to the Six Pillars. The Angel intelligence network is called 'The Watchers.'

The Demon Realm has no organized intelligence network. Demons rely on the Gnash trader network for information — Gnash who travel between realms bring back rumors, gossip, and observations. This makes demon intelligence unreliable but surprisingly comprehensive. The Mordrach also has 'Shadow Ears' — Scourge demons who spy on Bloodward commanders to prevent coups.

The Academy maintains its own intelligence apparatus: Instructors who monitor student activities and realm politics. The Academy's intelligence is the most accurate because it draws from all three realms simultaneously.

fields.label: Crown Eyes
fields.value: Human Realm — Veilrunner spies under Ruby Divina; operate in all three realms

fields.label: The Watchers
fields.value: Angel Realm — Lumen disguised as civilians; underestimated because they seem unimportant

fields.label: Shadow Ears
fields.value: Demon Realm — Scourge spying on Bloodward commanders; prevents coups

fields.label: Academy Intelligence
fields.value: Instructors monitor all three realms; most accurate cross-realm intelligence

name: The Assassin's Market
subtitle: Where killing is bought and sold
description:
Beyond the Broker's Guild's regulated termination contracts, an underground assassin's market exists in the Demon Realm.

The Blood Pit is an illegal marketplace beneath the Umbrage Forest where assassins, bounty hunters, and contract killers gather to sell their services. Unlike the Broker's Guild, the Blood Pit has no rules — anyone can hire anyone for any purpose. The only requirement is payment upfront.

The Blood Pit's most famous contractors are the Shadow Choir — a group of Veilrunner assassins who work as a unit. They specialize in killing D-rank and above targets, which puts them in high demand for political assassinations. Their fee starts at 100 Gold Crowns per target.

The Broker's Guild officially condemns the Blood Pit but secretly tolerates it — the Blood Pit handles contracts that the Guild won't touch (killing protected targets, political assassinations, realm destabilization). As long as the Blood Pit doesn't interfere with Guild business, the Guild looks the other way.

The most dangerous aspect of the Blood Pit is information trading — assassins sell not just their blades but their knowledge. Secrets about target weaknesses, realm security gaps, and political vulnerabilities are traded alongside killing contracts.

fields.label: Blood Pit
fields.value: Illegal marketplace beneath Umbrage Forest — no rules, payment upfront

fields.label: Shadow Choir
fields.value: Veilrunner assassin unit — D-rank+ targets, 100+ gc per contract

fields.label: Guild Tolerance
fields.value: Blood Pit handles contracts the Guild won't touch; unofficial cooperation

fields.label: Information Trading
fields.value: Assassins sell knowledge alongside blades — secrets about weaknesses and gaps

name: Information Brokers
subtitle: The people who sell secrets for a price
description:
Information Brokers are a specific subset of the Broker class who deal exclusively in secrets.

An Information Broker buys, holds, and sells intelligence — political secrets, military plans, personal scandals, magical research, anything with value. They are protected by the Broker's Guild because their trade is legal (selling information is not a crime; stealing it might be).

The most valuable information categories are: Military intelligence (troop movements, fortification plans), Magical research (new spells, enchantment techniques, Veyn discoveries), Political secrets (alliance negotiations, succession plans), and Personal leverage (compromising information on powerful individuals).

Information Brokers operate from fixed locations — usually a back room in a tavern or a hidden office in a market district. They never reveal their sources, and they never reveal who bought what. Breaking this code results in death.

The most famous Information Broker in the Half-Made World is known only as 'The Ledger' — an anonymous figure who has sold secrets to all three realms simultaneously without any realm knowing about the others. The Ledger's identity is the Half-Made World's greatest unsolved mystery.

fields.label: Information Brokers
fields.value: Buy, hold, sell intelligence — legal under Broker's Guild protection

fields.label: Valuable Categories
fields.value: Military, magical research, political secrets, personal leverage

fields.label: Operating Method
fields.value: Hidden offices in taverns/markets — sources and buyers never revealed

fields.label: The Ledger

name: The Holding Cells
subtitle: How criminals are imprisoned across realms
description:
Each realm handles imprisonment differently.

Human Realm prisons are stone-walled cells in the basement of Magistrate buildings. Common criminals (thieves, assaulters) serve time in communal cells — crowded, uncomfortable, but survivable. Serious criminals (murderers, magical criminals) are held in individual cells with Veyn-dampening runes carved into the walls, preventing them from using any magic. The most dangerous criminals are held in the Null Block — a section of the prison where the runes are strong enough to suppress even angel and demon abilities. Sentences range from days (minor theft) to life (murder).

The Angel Realm does not have prisons. Angels who break laws are punished through Vow-shaming — their broken Vow is broadcast to nearby angels, causing social ostracism. For serious crimes, the Serapharch can revoke an angel's Vow, effectively making them Fallen. This is considered a fate worse than imprisonment.

The Demon Realm has no prisons. Criminal punishment is immediate and violent — usually death or mutilation. The Mordrach decides the punishment personally. For minor offenses, the criminal may be forced into gladiatorial combat in the Obsidian Arena as entertainment.

The Academy has its own detention facility: a series of Veyn-dampened rooms in the basement where students who commit serious offenses are held. The Head Master personally reviews each case.

fields.label: Human Prisons
fields.value: Stone cells with Veyn-dampening runes; Null Block suppresses all magic

fields.label: Angel Punishment
fields.value: No prisons — Vow-shaming (social ostracism) or forced Fall for serious crimes

fields.label: Demon Punishment
fields.value: No prisons — death, mutilation, or forced gladiatorial combat

fields.label: Academy Detention
fields.value: Veyn-dampened basement rooms; Head Master reviews each case

name: Channel Severing
subtitle: The magical equivalent of the death penalty
description:
Channel Severing is the most feared punishment in the Half-Made World — worse than death for any fighter.

Channel Severing permanently destroys a person's Veyn or Ren channels — the internal pathways that allow them to use magic. Once severed, the channels cannot regenerate. The person becomes permanently unable to use any magical abilities, effectively reducing them to G-rank (no Veyn connection).

The process is performed by high-rank Exorcists using the Rite of Severance — a brutal procedure that involves channeling holy energy directly into the victim's channels, burning them from the inside out. The victim is conscious throughout the process and can feel their magic dying. The pain is described as 'having your soul burned away piece by piece.'

Channel Severing is reserved for the most serious crimes: murder, treason, forced Veyn tampering, and contract fraud. It is considered a more merciful alternative to death because the person lives, but it is widely regarded as crueler — a fighter without their magic is a person without their identity.

Some criminals prefer death to Channel Severing. The Academy has been known to offer Channel Severing as an alternative to execution for students who commit capital offenses, which has led to ethical debates about whether it is truly more merciful.

fields.label: What It Does
fields.value: Permanently destroys Veyn or Ren channels — reduces to G-rank, no magic ever again

fields.label: The Process
fields.value: Exorcists channel holy energy into victim's channels, burning them from inside

fields.label: Pain Level
fields.value: Conscious throughout — described as having your soul burned piece by piece

fields.label: Crimes Warranting
fields.value: Murder, treason, forced Veyn tampering, contract fraud

fields.label: Ethical Debate
fields.value: More merciful than death or crueler? Fighter without magic is person without identity

name: Human Realm Buildings
subtitle: How humans construct their world
description:
Human architecture ranges from simple to elaborate depending on wealth and function.

Common Housing: Mud-brick or timber-frame houses with thatched roofs. Single-story for laborers, two-story for skilled workers. interiors are cramped — one or two rooms for sleeping, cooking, and living. Windows are covered with oiled cloth, not glass. Heating comes from a central hearth; smoke exits through a hole in the roof.

Merchant Housing: Stone or brick buildings with glass windows (a luxury). Multi-room layouts with separate bedrooms, a kitchen, and a workshop or store. Interiors are decorated with woven tapestries, wooden furniture, and oil lamps. Some merchant homes have cellars for storing goods.

Noble Estates: Large compounds with stone walls, multiple buildings, courtyards, and gardens. Glass windows are standard. Interiors feature marble floors, painted walls, chandeliers, and imported furniture. Some estates include training grounds for guards and private meditation rooms for Veyn users.

Public Buildings: Magistrate buildings are imposing stone structures with columns and sealed doors. Taverns are wooden or stone with large common rooms, private rooms upstairs, and kitchens in the back. Temples are simple circular stone structures with Veyn Stone crystals at their centers.

The Capital City: The largest city in the Human Realm, built around the original Sundering Altar temple. Buildings are mostly stone, with the palace district featuring marble and gold accents. The Ashwell Colosseum is the city's most impressive structure — a massive circular arena that seats 10,000 spectators.

fields.value: Mud-brick/timber-frame, thatched roofs, oiled cloth windows, one or two rooms

fields.label: Merchant Housing
fields.value: Stone/brick, glass windows, multi-room with workshops and cellars

fields.label: Noble Estates
fields.value: Stone compounds with courtyards, gardens, training grounds, meditation rooms

fields.value: Magistrate stone columns, tavern wooden common rooms, circular temples

name: Angel Realm Architecture
subtitle: How angels build their cities
description:
Angel architecture is elegant, vertical, and infused with Veyn.

Angel cities are built upward rather than outward — towering spires of white stone connected by bridges and walkways. The highest spires belong to the Six Pillars; the lowest belong to Lumen workers. Height equals status in angel architecture.

Materials: Angel buildings are constructed from 'Dawnstone' — a white stone that absorbs Holy Energy and glows faintly at night. The stone is quarried from the Angel Realm's mountains and shaped using Veyn tools. Dawnstone resists weathering and can last thousands of years without maintenance.

Interiors: Angel interiors are minimal and functional. Angels do not accumulate possessions the way humans do. A typical angel home contains a meditation alcove, a sleeping platform, and little else. Higher-ranked angels have larger spaces but fill them with light rather than objects — walls that glow, ceilings that shimmer, windows that display visions of the outside world.

The Cathedral of the First Vow: The most important building in the Angel Realm — a massive spire where the first Vow was spoken. The interior walls are inscribed with the original Vow in Angel Script, and the light from the inscriptions fills the entire building with a warm, golden glow. Angels make pilgrimages here to reaffirm their vows.

fields.label: Vertical Cities
fields.value: Towering spires of white stone — height equals status

fields.label: Dawnstone
fields.value: White stone that absorbs Holy Energy, glows at night, lasts millennia

fields.label: Minimal Interiors

fields.label: Cathedral of First Vow

name: Demon Realm Architecture
subtitle: How demons build their strongholds
description:
Demon architecture is brutal, functional, and built to intimidate.

Demon cities are not planned — they grow organically from the center outward, each building constructed wherever the builder feels like putting it. The result is a chaotic maze of structures with no streets, no alleys, and no logical layout. Navigation requires local knowledge or territorial instinct.

Materials: Demon buildings are constructed from black stone quarried from the Umbrage Forest's volcanic regions, reinforced with corrupted Veyn. The stone is dark, rough, and absorbs light. Demon buildings are cold to the touch and feel oppressive to non-demons.

Interiors: Demon interiors are spartan and weapon-focused. A typical demon dwelling contains a sleeping area (usually just a pile of furs), a weapon rack, and a training space. Higher-ranked demons have larger spaces but fill them with trophies — skulls, weapons taken from defeated enemies, and pieces of armor from fallen rivals.

The Obsidian Arena: The Demon Realm's most important structure — a massive open-air arena where disputes are settled through combat, criminals are executed, and entertainment is provided through gladiatorial fights. The arena is carved from a single massive block of obsidian and can seat 50,000 spectators.

The Mordrach's Tower: A single black spire in the center of the Demon Realm capital where Tera Morage resides. The tower is surrounded by a field of corrupted Veyn that kills any unauthorized visitor.

fields.value: No planning — cities grow organically, navigation requires local knowledge

fields.value: Weapon racks, training spaces, trophy collections — nothing decorative

name: Veyn Skill Activation Guide
subtitle: How each Veyn-based class activates their skills
description:
Veyn-based skills follow a three-step activation process: Draw, Shape, Release.

DRAW: The user pulls ambient Veyn into their channels through concentration and intent. This takes 0.5-3 seconds depending on the skill's complexity and the user's grade. F-rank Mages take 2-3 seconds; A-rank Mages take under 0.5 seconds.

SHAPE: The user mentally shapes the drawn Veyn into the desired effect — a bolt, a shield, a healing wave, an enchantment. Shaping requires knowledge of the skill's specific pattern, which is learned through training. Simple shapes (bolts, basic shields) are intuitive; complex shapes (area healing, layered barriers) require years of practice.

RELEASE: The user releases the shaped Veyn in the desired direction or target. Release can be triggered by incantation (verbal command), gesture (hand movement), or thought (mental command at higher ranks). The release point is when the skill actually takes effect.

Cooldown: After release, the channels need 1-5 seconds to stabilize before another Draw can begin. During cooldown, the user is vulnerable. Skilled fighters learn to overlap cooldowns — beginning the Draw for the next skill while the previous skill is still resolving.

Veyn Cost: Each skill consumes a portion of the user's Veyn reserves. Basic skills cost 1-5% of reserves; ultimate skills can cost 50% or more. Running out of Veyn mid-combat leaves the user helpless until they can rest and replenish.

fields.label: Step 1: Draw
fields.value: Pull ambient Veyn into channels — 0.5 to 3 seconds depending on grade

fields.label: Step 2: Shape
fields.value: Mentally shape Veyn into the effect — requires learned skill patterns

fields.label: Step 3: Release
fields.value: Trigger by incantation, gesture, or thought — skill takes effect

fields.label: Cooldown
fields.value: 1-5 seconds between casts — user is vulnerable during stabilization

fields.label: Veyn Cost
fields.value: Basic 1-5% reserves; ultimates 50%+ — running out leaves user helpless

name: Ren Skill Activation Guide
subtitle: How each Ren-based class activates their skills
description:
Ren-based skills follow a different process: Channel, Focus, Burst.

CHANNEL: The user pushes Vitality from their core outward through their body. Unlike Veyn which is drawn from outside, Ren is pushed from inside — it feels warm, physical, and draining. Channeling takes less conscious effort than Veyn drawing because the energy is already inside the body.

FOCUS: The user directs the channeled Vitality to the desired body part or weapon. A Berserker channels to their muscles for enhanced strength; a Sentinel channels to their skin for iron defense; a Bladesinger channels to their sword for enhanced cutting power. Focusing requires physical awareness — knowing exactly where your body needs the energy.

BURST: The user releases the focused Vitality in a sudden surge. Unlike Veyn's controlled release, Ren bursts are explosive and immediate — the power goes from internal to external in an instant. This is why Ren combat feels fast and physical while Veyn combat feels deliberate and controlled.

Exhaustion: Ren depletes Vitality, which is finite and replenishes slowly through rest and food. A Berserker who burns through their Vitality collapses — their muscles stop responding, their vision darkens, and they cannot move until they recover. Unlike Veyn users who can replenish from the environment, Ren users must rest for hours or days.

Self-Damage: Overusing Ren causes physical harm — torn muscles, burst blood vessels, and in extreme cases, organ failure. The Berserker's Mad Rampage skill explicitly accepts this damage as the cost of power.

fields.label: Step 1: Channel
fields.value: Push Vitality from core outward — warm, physical, less conscious effort than Veyn

fields.label: Step 2: Focus
fields.value: Direct Vitality to desired body part or weapon — requires physical awareness

fields.label: Step 3: Burst
fields.value: Explosive immediate release — internal to external in an instant

fields.label: Exhaustion
fields.value: Vitality depletion causes collapse — must rest hours or days to recover

fields.label: Self-Damage
fields.value: Overuse causes torn muscles, burst vessels, organ failure at extreme levels

name: Holy & Corrupted Skill Activation
subtitle: How purified and corrupted Veyn skills work
description:
Holy and Corrupted skills modify the basic Veyn activation process.

Holy Skills: The user draws raw Veyn and then purifies it through their own conviction and intent. The purification process adds an extra step — after Draw, the user must 'Brighten' the Veyn, transforming it from neutral silver-blue to gold. This requires strong moral conviction and clear purpose. A Saintess who doubts herself cannot purify Veyn; her spells fail or come out weakened. The Brightening step adds 0.5-1 second to the casting time but produces effects that burn corruption on contact.

Corrupted Skills: The user draws raw Veyn and then corrupts it through rage, hatred, or demonic nature. The corruption step — called 'Darkening' — transforms Veyn from neutral silver-blue to deep purple or black. For demons, this is natural and requires no special effort; their Veyn channels are inherently corrupting. For humans attempting corrupted skills, the Darkening process damages their own channels over time, potentially triggering Corruption Sickness.

Dual-Aspect Skills: Vireth, the Fallen Grace, is the only weapon that channels both Holy and Corrupted Veyn simultaneously through a skill called Split Grace. This is theoretically impossible for any individual to achieve naturally — the Veyn would cancel itself out. Vireth's unique corrupted-divine nature allows it to bypass this restriction.

fields.label: Holy Brightening
fields.value: Extra step after Draw — purify Veyn to gold through conviction; adds 0.5-1 second

fields.label: Holy Failure
fields.value: Doubt weakens or fails the spell — moral conviction is required for purification

fields.label: Corrupt Darkening
fields.value: Transforms Veyn to purple/black; natural for demons, damages human channels over time

fields.label: Human Corruption Risk
fields.value: Humans using corrupted skills risk Corruption Sickness from channel damage

fields.label: Dual-Aspect
fields.value: Vireth only — channels both simultaneously; naturally impossible for individuals

name: The Creation of the World
subtitle: How the world came to be according to the World Core Faith
description:
According to the World Core Faith, the world began as a single point of infinite Veyn — a compressed seed of magical energy that contained everything that would ever exist. The seed cracked open, and the Veyn spilled outward, forming the physical world — land, water, sky, and life.

The world core remained at the center, still dreaming, still generating Veyn. Everything in the world — every person, every creature, every tree and stone — is made of Veyn shaped by the core's dreams. When the core dreams of life, living things grow. When the core dreams of death, living things end.

The first beings were the Aelthar — beings of pure Veyn who could shape reality with their thoughts. They built the Shudon to maintain the world while the core slept. They discovered the World Eater — a parasite that had latched onto the core during the initial crack, slowly draining it. They created the Hidden Realm to redirect the World Eater's feeding.

When the Hidden Realm was created, the resulting Veyn disruption split the world into three realms and nearly destroyed everything. The Aelthar were wiped out in the catastrophe. Their Echoes still fight on the battlefield where they fell.

The core continued to dream. New beings emerged — humans, angels, demons, elves. The Sundering Altars were built to help these new beings access the Veyn that had always been inside them. And the world continued, fragile and half-made, waiting for the core to finally wake up.

fields.label: The Seed
fields.value: Infinite Veyn compressed into a single point — cracked open to form the world

fields.label: The World Core
fields.value: Center of the world, still dreaming, generating all Veyn

fields.label: The Aelthar
fields.value: First beings — pure Veyn, built Shudon, discovered World Eater

fields.label: The Sundering
fields.value: Hidden Realm creation split the world into three realms — Aelthar destroyed

fields.label: The Dream
fields.value: Core continues to dream — new beings emerge, world continues, waiting for awakening

name: The Fall of the Aelthar
subtitle: How the original rulers were destroyed
description:
The Aelthar were not destroyed in a single battle — they were destroyed by their own solution to the World Eater.

When the Aelthar discovered the World Eater draining the core, they debated for centuries on how to stop it. Some argued for direct confrontation — attacking the World Eater itself. Others argued for retreat — creating a separate realm where they could survive while the core slowly died. The debate split the Aelthar into factions.

The winning faction decided to create the Hidden Realm — a pocket dimension that would draw the World Eater's feeding away from the main core. The process required channeling enormous amounts of Veyn from the world core itself, which weakened the core significantly.

But the creation went wrong. The force required to split reality was far greater than anticipated. The Veyn backlash nearly destroyed the entire world — the Void Colossus appeared at the breach point, attacking everything nearby. The Aelthar fought to close the breach and contain the damage, but the cost was catastrophic.

By the time the breach was sealed, most of the Aelthar were dead. Their bodies dissolved into pure Veyn, returning to the world core. Their Echoes — the residual will of their final battle — remained on the battlefield, fighting an endless war that had already ended.

The survivors — a handful of Aelthar who had opposed the creation — were hunted down by the former Human Realm ruler and killed. The Aelthar were extinct within a generation of the Sundering.

fields.label: The Debate
fields.value: Centuries of argument — confront the World Eater or retreat to Hidden Realm

fields.label: The Creation
fields.value: Required channeling Veyn from the core — weakened it significantly

fields.label: The Backlash
fields.value: Force to split reality exceeded expectations — Void Colossus appeared

fields.label: The Cost
fields.value: Most Aelthar dead, bodies dissolved into Veyn; Echoes remain fighting on battlefield

fields.label: The Survivors
fields.value: Opposing faction hunted down by Human Realm ruler — Aelthar extinct within a generation

name: The Sealing of Vireth
subtitle: How the corrupted divine sword was bound
description:
The story of Vireth's sealing is one of the most retold tales in the Half-Made World, though the details are disputed.

Vireth, the Fallen Grace, was once a divine sword of pure Holy Energy — a weapon forged by the Aelthar to fight the World Eater. It was wielded by the greatest Aelthar warrior, who used it to seal the World Eater's physical manifestation. But during the battle, the sword was exposed to the World Eater's corruption — the same nullifying energy that drains Veyn from everything it touches.

The corruption twisted Vireth from a weapon of light into a weapon of both light and darkness. Its wielder, unable to control the corrupted blade, was consumed by it. The sword became sentient — a hungry thing that fed on Veyn and corrupted everything it cut.

The remaining Aelthar knew they could not destroy Vireth — it was too powerful. Instead, they chose the Sentient River — a living waterway that could sense intent and resist corruption. They convinced the river to accept the sword as a prisoner, and the river agreed, sealing Vireth beneath its waters under two separate seals.

The first seal was placed by the Aelthar using their combined Veyn. The second seal was placed by the river itself — its own awareness forming a barrier that Vireth cannot breach as long as the river maintains its vigilance.

The Sirens were bound to the river as additional guardians — their hypnotic song keeping the sword's influence contained. Together, the two seals and the Sirens form a triple-layered prison that has held Vireth for millennia.

fields.label: Origin
fields.value: Divine sword forged by Aelthar to fight the World Eater — corrupted during battle

fields.label: Sentience
fields.value: Became hungry, fed on Veyn, corrupted everything it cut — too powerful to destroy

fields.label: The Sealing
fields.value: Bound in the Sentient River — a living waterway that senses intent and resists corruption

fields.label: Double Seal
fields.value: First seal: Aelthar combined Veyn; Second seal: the river's own awareness

fields.label: Sirens
fields.value: Bound as additional guardians — hypnotic song contains the sword's influence

name: The Founding of Elyndor Academy
subtitle: How Kael von Ashen built the institution that shapes the world
description:
Kael von Ashen was not always the Head Master. He was once a Shudonkeeper — a scholar who studied the inactive Shudon and the Aelthar knowledge they carried.

Kael spent centuries in the Academy's precursor — a small research outpost near the Aelthar battlefield — studying the Echoes and the ruins. He discovered fragments of Aelthar texts that described the Sundering Altar's mechanism: a device that could unlock the Veyn connection in any living being.

Using this knowledge, Kael built the first Sundering Altar — the Common Altar in the neutral zone between realms. It was crude compared to the Academy Altar, but it worked. Children who underwent awakening at the Altar gained access to their Veyn for the first time.

The success of the Common Altar attracted attention from all three realms. Humans, angels, and demons all sent their children to be awakened. Kael realized that the Altar was more than a tool — it was a bridge between the realms. He founded Elyndor Academy around the second, more powerful Altar, and established the neutrality that has protected it ever since.

Kael's secret knowledge of the Aelthar, the Shudon, and the World Eater has been passed down through the Head Master position for millennia. Every Head Master learns the truth: the world is dying, the World Eater is draining the core, and the Shudon will eventually reawaken to stop it — but not before the world has been changed forever.

fields.value: Former Shudonkeeper who discovered Aelthar texts about the Altar mechanism

fields.label: First Altar
fields.value: Common Altar built in neutral zone — crude but functional; drew all three realms

fields.label: Academy Founding
fields.value: Second, more powerful Altar surrounded by Academy; neutrality established

fields.label: Secret Knowledge
fields.value: Passed to every Head Master: World Eater is draining core, Shudon will reawaken

fields.label: Altar as Bridge
fields.value: More than a tool — it connected all three realms through shared awakening

name: Weapon Catalog
subtitle: Every weapon type in the Half-Made World
description:
Weapons in the Half-Made World range from mundane to legendary.

Mundane Weapons: Daggers (2sm), Short Swords (1gc), Longswords (3-5gc), Axes (2-4gc), Maces (2-3gc), Spears (1-3gc), Bows (2-4gc), Crossbows (5-8gc). These are mass-produced by Smiths and available in any marketplace. They break under heavy Veyn or Ren channeling.

Enchanted Weapons: Created by Enchanters who imbue mundane weapons with Veyn effects. Enchanted weapons cost 10-50gc depending on the enchantment. Common enchantments include Fire Edge (adds burning damage), Frost Guard (slows attackers), and Veyn Conduit (improves Veyn channeling through the weapon).

Blood-Forged Weapons: Created by Smiths using demon or angel blood in the forge. The rank of the blood determines the weapon's power — low-rank blood can injure, high-rank blood can kill. Blood-forged weapons cost 50-200gc and are highly regulated by the Broker's Guild.

Divine Weapons: The most powerful weapons in existence. Only three exist: Vireth (corrupted divine sword), Virastra (uncorrupted divine sword), and Solvane (divine spear). Each is user-bound — they only work for their chosen wielder. Divine weapons cannot be bought, only found or inherited.

Named Weapons: Unique weapons with histories and personalities. Aerendrel (storm bow), Liework's Fallen Crown (command crown), and other artifacts fall into this category.

name: Armor Catalog
subtitle: Protective equipment across the realms
description:
Armor in the Half-Made World must balance protection with mobility.

Light Armor: Leather armor (5sm) offers basic protection against slashes and blunt force. Studded leather (8sm) adds metal rivets for extra defense. Light armor allows full mobility and does not interfere with Veyn or Ren channeling. Preferred by Veilrunners, Archers, and Alchemists.

Medium Armor: Chain mail (5gc) provides excellent protection against slashing weapons and moderate protection against piercing. It is heavy but flexible enough for active combat. Preferred by Bladesingers, Berserkers, and general soldiers.

Heavy Armor: Plate armor (50-100gc) provides maximum protection but severely limits mobility. A full suit of plate weighs 40-60 pounds and makes climbing, swimming, and sneaking nearly impossible. Preferred by Sentinels and elite guards. Plate armor can be enchanted to reduce weight and improve Veyn conductivity.

Magical Armor: Enchanted by Enchanters or Smiths with protective Veyn effects. Examples include Shieldward Plate (generates a Veyn barrier on impact), Miasma-Resistant Chain (reduces Corruption Sickness risk), and Featherlight Leather (reduces weight by 80%). Magical armor costs 2-10x the base price.

Demon Armor: Corrupted Veyn-infused armor unique to the Demon Realm. Black iron plate, bone-reinforced leather, and chain made from monster parts. Demon armor often enhances the wearer's demonic aura but harms non-demon users over time.

name: Tool & Utility Items
subtitle: Non-combat equipment for adventuring
description:
Beyond weapons and armor, adventurers carry tools for survival.

Remy's Bracelet (already cataloged): Stores up to 10 items, activated by Veyn/Ren.

Veyn Compass: A small device that points toward the nearest source of concentrated Veyn. Used by adventurers navigating the Ether Forest, Hidden Realm, or any Veyn-rich area. Costs 10-15gc.

Exorcist Lantern: A lantern powered by holy energy that reveals hidden spirits, illusions, and corrupted Veyn. Essential for navigating areas with undead or spirit activity. Costs 20-30gc.

Purification Tablets: Small tablets of compressed holy energy that can be dissolved in water to create a single-use purification solution. Used to cleanse minor Corruption Sickness or purify contaminated water. Costs 5gc per tablet.

Mapping Stones: Crystals that record the Veyn signature of a location, allowing the holder to return to that exact spot by following the stored signature. Essentially a magical GPS. Costs 15-20gc.

Echo Crystals: Recording devices that capture and replay sounds. Used by scholars, spies, and intelligence gatherers. A single crystal can store up to one hour of audio. Costs 8-12gc.

name: Tavern Culture
subtitle: The social hubs of the Half-Made World
description:
Taverns are the most important social spaces in the Human Realm — where news spreads, deals are made, and fights break out.

Tavern Anatomy: A typical tavern has a large common room with wooden tables and benches, a bar counter staffed by the tavern keeper, a kitchen in the back, and private rooms upstairs for lodging. The common room is where the action happens — eating, drinking, gambling, storytelling, and occasionally brawling.

Tavern Keepers: The most well-informed people in any town. They hear every rumor, witness every deal, and know every traveler who passes through. Smart adventurers cultivate relationships with tavern keepers — a free drink buys useful information. Most tavern keepers are former adventurers themselves, retired after injuries or wealth accumulation.

Tavern Rules: Fighting in a tavern is technically illegal, but tavern keepers rarely enforce it unless property is damaged. The unspoken rule is: fight outside, pay for what you break, and don't hurt the staff. Breaking these rules gets you banned from the tavern — a social death sentence in small towns where the tavern is the only gathering place.

Tavern Music: Most taverns have a resident musician or invite traveling performers. Common songs tell stories of heroes, monsters, and lost loves. The most famous tavern song is 'The Ballad of the Wanderer' — a haunting melody about the immortal merchant who walks between realms.

Tavern Food: Simple and filling — stew, bread, cheese, roasted meat, ale. The tavern keeper's stew recipe is often a closely guarded secret. Specialties vary by region: coastal taverns serve fish, mountain taverns serve game, and forest taverns serve Ether Forest mushrooms.

name: The Resting Stone Inn Chain
subtitle: The most famous inn network in the Human Realm
description:
The Resting Stone is the most recognized inn chain in the Human Realm — a series of identical inns along the Sunward Road, each offering the same menu and prices regardless of location.

Every Resting Stone inn has the same layout: a large common room, a bar, a kitchen, 10 private rooms, and a stable. The menu is standardized — bread and stew for 5cp, ale for 2cp, a private room for 1sm. The consistency is the brand — travelers know exactly what to expect.

The chain was founded by a former Broker who realized that travelers valued predictability over luxury. The founding principle was: 'A good night's rest should cost the same whether you're in the capital or at the border.'

Resting Stone innkeepers are trained by the chain's central office and are required to maintain standards. A Resting Stone that fails health or service inspections is shut down and the innkeeper replaced. This quality control has made the chain the most trusted accommodation in the Human Realm.

The chain has 47 locations along the Sunward Road and 12 in major cities off the road. Expansion into the Angel Realm is planned but complicated by angel dietary differences.

name: Political Factions
subtitle: The power blocs competing for influence
description:
Several political factions compete for influence across the three realms.

The Purists (Human Realm): A conservative faction that believes only humans should rule the Human Realm. They oppose angel and demon influence in human affairs and want to close the Realm Gates permanently. Led by Lord Malachar, a noble who lost family to demon raids. The Purists are popular among commoners who fear demonic corruption.

The Integrationists (Human Realm): A progressive faction that believes all three realms should work together under the Academy's leadership. They support cross-realm trade, cultural exchange, and joint military operations against shared threats. Led by Lady Seraphine, a diplomat who has negotiated trade agreements with both angels and demons.

The Vow Keepers (Angel Realm): A militant angel faction that believes the angels should reclaim their ancient role as world guardians. They want to reactivate the Shudon and enforce angel law across all three realms. Led by Archangel Veradis, one of the Six Pillars who believes the current peace is weakening the angels.

The Severed (Angel Realm): A radical faction of former angels who have voluntarily broken their Vows. They believe the Vow system is a form of control and that angels should be free to choose their own path. They operate from hidden bases in the Human Realm.

The Blood Pack (Demon Realm): A war-band coalition that wants to replace the Mordrach's rule with a council of Bloodwards. They believe the Mordrach has grown too passive and that the Demon Realm should expand aggressively. Led by Bloodward Drakar, who has been quietly building support among mid-rank demons.

name: Realm Relations
subtitle: How the three realms interact diplomatically
description:
The three realms maintain a tense peace enforced by mutual dependency.

Human-Angel Relations: The strongest alliance. Angels provide military protection; humans provide food, labor, and trade goods. The relationship is genuine but unequal — humans need angel protection more than angels need human goods. The Purists resent this dependency; the Integrationists embrace it.

Human-Demon Relations: The most volatile. Trade exists along the Thorn Road, but raids, smuggling, and cultural hostility keep tensions high. The Broker's Guild mediates most disputes, but border incidents occasionally escalate to military confrontation. Most humans fear and distrust demons.

Angel-Demon Relations: The most hostile. Angels and demons are ideological opposites — Holy Energy vs Corrupted Veyn, Vow-keeping vs contract-making, order vs chaos. Open warfare has not occurred in centuries, but intelligence operations and proxy conflicts are constant. The Academy's neutrality prevents direct confrontation.

The Academy's Role: The Academy serves as the only neutral ground where all three realms interact peacefully. It is the only institution that all three rulers recognize and respect. Attacking the Academy would unite all three realms against the attacker — which is why no realm has ever tried.

The Hidden Realm Factor: The Hidden Realm is wild card — its portal moves unpredictably, its inhabitants are independent, and its resources are invaluable. Every realm wants control of the Hidden Realm; none can achieve it.

name: Banking & Financial Systems
subtitle: How money is stored, lent, and managed
description:
The Half-Made World has a rudimentary banking system centered in the Human Realm's capital.

The Vault of Ashwell is the largest and most trusted bank in the world. Founded by a consortium of merchant families, it accepts deposits, issues loans, and handles large transactions between realms. Depositors receive a sealed letter of credit — a document that can be redeemed at any Vault branch across the Human Realm.

Loan System: The Vault issues loans at interest rates determined by the borrower's grade and creditworthiness. Commoners pay 20-30% annual interest; merchants pay 10-15%; nobles pay 5-8%. Defaulting on a loan results in asset seizure — the Vault's enforcers (high-rank Veilrunners) will take possessions, property, and in extreme cases, enforce labor until the debt is repaid.

Letters of Credit: Paper documents that represent a specific amount of gold deposited in the Vault. They are lighter and safer than carrying coin — a letter worth 100 Gold Crowns weighs nothing compared to 100 physical coins. Merchants use letters of credit for large transactions. Forgery is punished by permanent exile.

The Vault's Secret: The Vault of Ashwell maintains a secret reserve of Aelthar artifacts and knowledge, accumulated over centuries. This reserve is known only to the Vault's inner council and has never been disclosed to any realm authority. The Vault's true power comes not from its gold but from its secrets.

name: Debt & Indentured Service
subtitle: How poverty traps people in the Half-Made World
description:
Debt is one of the most common forms of social control in the Human Realm.

Indentured Service: When a commoner cannot pay their debts, they can sign an indenture contract — a Broker-sealed agreement that binds them to work for their creditor for a fixed period (usually 1-5 years). During indenture, the worker receives no wages and cannot leave without permission. Breaking an indenture contract carries the same Veyn-channel damage as any other Broker-sealed contract.

Debt Traps: Many commoners fall into debt cycles — borrowing to pay for medical treatment, then borrowing more to pay off the first loan. The Vault of Ashwell's interest rates ensure that debt grows faster than a commoner's income. Some families have been in debt for generations.

Debt Slavery: The most extreme form of debt — a permanent indenture where the debtor works for the creditor for life. This is technically illegal in the Human Realm, but the law is rarely enforced against wealthy creditors. The practice is common in the Demon Realm, where Gnash demons are born into debt to their Bloodward overlords.

Anti-Debt Movements: The Integrationist faction has proposed debt forgiveness laws, but these have been blocked by the Merchant Class who profit from the current system. Some radical groups advocate for violent debt abolition, but these movements are suppressed by the Magistrates.

name: The Black Market Economy
subtitle: Illegal trade and underground commerce
description:
The black market in the Half-Made World is vast and organized, primarily operating through the Demon Realm's Umbrage Forest border.

Corrupted Veyn Trade: The most profitable illegal trade. Corrupted artifacts, miasma-infused weapons, and tainted Veyn stones are smuggled from the Demon Realm into the Human Realm, where they sell at 5-10x their value. Exorcists actively hunt smugglers, but the profits are too high to stop completely.

Information Trade: Secrets about realm politics, military movements, and Academy research are traded between realms. The most valuable intelligence is information about the Shudon — any detail about reactivation is worth a fortune.

Creature Trade: Rare creatures and their parts are captured and sold illegally. Pixie dust (smuggled from the Hidden Realm), dragon hearts (harvested from killed dragons), and Stonehollow Elk antlers (illegally poached) are among the most valuable. The Pallantine Rangers actively combat creature poaching in the Arubian Forest.

The Black Market's Leader: No single person controls the black market, but the closest thing is a figure known as 'The Masked Coin' — an anonymous Gnash who operates from the Umbrage Forest and coordinates smuggling routes across all three realms. The Masked Coin has never been identified and is believed to work with the knowledge of the Broker's Guild.

name: Agricultural Systems
subtitle: How food is produced across the realms
description:
Agriculture is the foundation of the Human Realm's economy.

The Human Realm has vast farmlands between the capital and the Ether Forest border. The most common crops are wheat, barley, root vegetables (potatoes, turnips, carrots), and orchard fruits (apples, pears, plums). Farming is done by the Common Class using animal-drawn plows and manual labor. Veyn-enhanced farming exists but is rare — wealthy landowners use Mages to enrich soil and accelerate crop growth, but most farmers cannot afford this.

Crop yields vary by season and Veyn density. Farms near the Ether Forest produce larger, more nutrient-rich crops because of ambient Veyn exposure. Farms at the edges of the Human Realm produce smaller yields because Veyn density is lower.

The Angel Realm does not farm traditionally. Angels draw sustenance directly from ambient Veyn, which means they need very little food. Lumen who choose to eat cultivate small gardens of fruits and herbs, but this is cultural, not necessity.

The Demon Realm has no agriculture. Demons eat what they kill. Gnash traders occasionally purchase food from human merchants, but most demons consider buying food a weakness.

The Hidden Realm has no agriculture — time dilation makes traditional farming impractical. Travelers survive on packed rations or hunted game.

name: Mining & Raw Materials
subtitle: Where metals, stones, and Veyn resources come from
description:
The Half-Made World's raw materials come from distinct sources.

Metals: Iron, copper, tin, and gold are mined from mountain ranges in all three realms. The Human Realm's Ashvein Mountains are the largest mining region, producing iron and copper. Silver comes from the Angel Realm's Moonpeak range. Gold is rare and found only in deep mines in the Demon Realm's volcanic regions.

Veyn Stones: Crystallized Veyn found in areas of high Veyn density — primarily the Ether Forest, the Hidden Realm, and near the Sundering Altar. Veyn Stones are mined by Enchanters and Alchemists who need them for potions and enchantments. Lucent Stones are refined from Veyn Stones through a purification process that requires multiple days of Veyn exposure.

Monster Parts: Bones, scales, blood, venom, and organs from monsters are valuable crafting materials. Trolls bones are used for building reinforcement; Dragon scales are used for armor; Manticore venom sacs are used for paralytic poisons; Chimera blood is used for explosive compounds.

Ether Forest Resources: The Arubian Forest produces rare herbs, mushrooms, and plant materials used in Alchemy. Sunpetal flowers, Thornmoss, and Everbloom vines are gathered by Pallantine Elves and sold to human merchants. The Umbrage Forest produces corrupted materials — Blackthorn, Ironvine, and corrupted Veyn crystals.

Ebonspire Trees: Found near dragon nests in the Hidden Realm. Their bark and leaves are ingredients for the Ethereal Potion and Rejuvenating Elixir.

name: Alchemy & Potion Brewing
subtitle: How alchemical items are created
description:
Alchemy is the art of combining Veyn with physical ingredients to create potions, poisons, and explosives. It is one of the most practical and dangerous classes.

Brewing Process: An Alchemist draws Veyn into a mortar, pestle, or brewing vessel, then adds physical ingredients in a specific sequence. The Veyn reacts with the ingredients, transforming them into the desired effect. The sequence matters — adding ingredients in the wrong order can produce poison instead of healing, or cause an explosion.

Common Potions:
- Healing Potion (5-10sm): Heals minor to moderate injuries. Ingredients: Veyn Stone dust, medicinal herbs, clean water.
- Restoration Potion (10-15gc): Restores Veyn reserves. Ingredients: Multiple Veyn Stones, rare herbs.
- Paralytic Venom (50+gc): Paralyzes targets up to C-rank. Ingredients: Manticore venom sac, Veyn catalyst.
- Purification Solution (5gc per dose): Cleanses minor Corruption Sickness. Ingredients: Holy herbs, purified Veyn.
- Explosive Mix (20gc): Creates a blast on impact. Ingredients: Chimera blood, Veyn Stone dust, sulfur.

Advanced Potions:
- Lucent Reserve (50+gc): Full restoration of Veyn or Ren. Requires Lucent Stone.
- Ethereal Potion (priceless): Halts aging for a fixed period. Requires pixie dust, Grimbough leaves, Ebonspire bark, dragon heart.
- Rejuvenating Elixir (priceless): Complete healing of any wound. Ebonspire leaves.

Danger: Botched brews can cause explosions, poison the brewer, or release corrupted Veyn. Every Alchemist has scars from failed brews.

name: Monster Ecosystems
subtitle: How creatures interact in the food chain
description:
The Half-Made World's monsters form complex ecosystems, especially in the Ether Forest.

Arubian Forest Ecosystem: The light side of the forest has a balanced food chain. Fairies at the bottom (pollinate plants, guide travelers for trade), Pallantine Elves as stewards, Griffens as apex predators of the sky, and Stonehollow Elk as mega-herbivores whose shed antlers feed the Veyn cycle. Thornweald spirits protect the oldest trees, maintaining forest health.

Umbrage Forest Ecosystem: The dark side is a brutal survival environment. Goblins at the bottom (trappers, scavengers), Trolls and Orcs as mid-tier predators, Minotaurs as aggressive territorial hunters, Harpies as aerial ambush predators, and Dragons as apex predators. The ecosystem is driven by competition — creatures fight for territory and food constantly.

Hidden Realm Ecosystem: Unique because of time dilation. Creatures age slower, allowing ancient specimens to persist. Pixies are passive prey; Dragons are apex predators; the Coilmane guards Thornlost Forest. The ecosystem is isolated — no creatures naturally move between the Hidden Realm and the main three.

Monster Harvesting: Many creatures are hunted for resources. Dragon hearts for Ethereal Potions, Manticore venom sacs for poisons, Basilisk eyes for enchantments, Chimera blood for explosives. This creates an economic incentive for monster hunting, which in turn affects population dynamics — too much hunting can collapse a species, too little can lead to overpopulation.

name: Monster Behavior Patterns
subtitle: How creatures hunt, defend, and survive
description:
Understanding monster behavior is essential for survival.

Territorial Creatures: Dragons, Coilmane, and Basilisks are strictly territorial. They mark their territory through scent, Veyn markers, or physical destruction. Entering a territorial creature's range triggers aggression — they do not warn, they attack. The only exception is the Coilmane, which allows passage if the traveler demonstrates peaceful intent.

Pack Hunters: Trolls, Goblins, and Orcs hunt in groups. They use coordinated tactics — flanking, encirclement, and baiting. Troll packs use size advantage; Goblin warrens use traps and numbers; Orc war-bands use brute force coordination. Facing any of these alone is survivable; facing a pack is lethal.

Ambush Predators: Manticores, Basilisks, and Cockatrices rely on stealth and surprise. They remain hidden until prey is within striking distance. Manticores bury themselves in soil; Basilisks coil in undergrowth; Cockatrices use lure-and-flank tactics. Awareness and counter-detection are the best defenses.

Passive Creatures: Pixies, Fairies, Lightwisps, and Stonetenders are non-aggressive. They flee from danger or ignore it entirely. Harming these creatures has social and environmental consequences.

Corrupted Creatures: Werewolves and other corrupted beings are driven by compulsion, not strategy. They attack anything in range during transformation. The only defense is avoidance or overwhelming force.

name: Academy Daily Life
subtitle: What students experience at Elyndor Academy
description:
Life at Elyndor Academy is structured, competitive, and transformative.

Daily Schedule: Students wake at dawn, meditate for Veyn/Ren attunement, attend classes in the morning, train in the afternoon, and study in the evening. Meals are communal — served in the Great Hall where all races eat together. This enforced integration is intentional — the Academy believes familiarity breeds tolerance.

Classes: Academic subjects (history, theory, ethics) are taught in the morning. Practical training (combat, spellcasting, forging) happens in the afternoon. Students are assigned to Instructors based on their class affinity — a Mage student trains with a Mage Instructor, a Berserker with a Berserker Instructor.

Competition: Students are ranked by performance in training and academic assessment. The top-ranked student in each year is awarded the 'Ashen Star' — a medal that carries significant prestige after graduation. Competition is fierce but regulated — cheating results in immediate expulsion.

Housing: Students sleep in dormitories organized by class affinity. Mixed dorms are available for students who want cross-class friendships. Private rooms are available for upper-ranked students.

The Head Master's Address: Once a month, the Head Master addresses the entire student body in the Great Hall. Topics range from Academy policy to world events. Students are encouraged to ask questions — the Head Master answers honestly, though some answers are deliberately vague.

fields.label: Daily Schedule
fields.value: Dawn meditation → morning classes → afternoon training → evening study → communal meals

fields.label: Class Structure
fields.value: Academic mornings, practical afternoons — Instructors assigned by class affinity

name: Academy Instructors
subtitle: The teachers who shape the next generation
description:
Academy Instructors are among the most accomplished fighters and scholars in the world.

Selection: Instructors are chosen by the Head Master based on three criteria: combat ability (minimum B-rank), teaching aptitude (ability to explain complex concepts simply), and realm diversity (the Academy maintains representation from all three realms among its faculty).

Instructor Roles: Each Instructor specializes in a specific class and teaches all students with that affinity. A Mage Instructor teaches all Mage students; a Berserker Instructor teaches all Berserker students. Some Instructors teach cross-class electives — subjects that multiple classes can benefit from.

Notable Instructors: The Academy currently has 19 Instructors (one per class), plus several cross-class specialists. The most senior Instructor is Master Theron, a former Paladin who has taught at the Academy for over 200 years. The most controversial is Instructor Nyx, a Veilrunner who was recruited from the Demon Realm and teaches stealth and infiltration.

Instructor Authority: Instructors have significant authority over their students — they can assign extra training, restrict privileges, and in extreme cases, recommend expulsion. The Head Master has final say on all disciplinary matters.

Instructor Independence: Instructors are free to develop their own teaching methods. Some are strict disciplinarians; others are hands-off mentors. This freedom attracts top talent but occasionally creates conflicts between Instructors with different philosophies.

fields.value: One per class specialty; some teach cross-class electives

name: Academy Examinations
subtitle: How students are tested and graduated
description:
Academy examinations determine a student's rank, progression, and eventual graduation.

Entrance Examination: Students are tested when they first arrive at age 15. The Academy Altar determines their class affinity and starting grade. Students with insufficient Veyn/Ren potential are sent home — roughly 20% of applicants fail this initial test.

Annual Assessments: Every year, students undergo two assessments — an academic examination (theory, ethics, history) and a practical examination (combat, skill execution, real-world application). Results determine the student's rank within their year.

Trial by Thornlost: The most feared examination. Students are sent into the Thornlost Forest in the Hidden Realm with minimal supplies and must survive for one week. The Coilmane patrols the forest, monsters roam freely, and the time-slowed environment means the week feels like two months. This trial tests not just combat ability but survival instincts, decision-making, and mental resilience.

Graduation Requirements: Students graduate when they reach D-rank (or equivalent for Mages) and complete the Trial by Thornlost. Graduation takes an average of 3-5 years, though some students take longer and others are expelled before completing.

Post-Graduation: Graduates receive a certificate of completion and are recognized across all three realms. The Academy's alumni network is one of the most powerful social structures in the world — Academy graduates hold positions of power in every realm.

name: Fighter Training Methods
subtitle: How warriors develop their skills
description:
Combat training in the Half-Made World varies by class and realm.

Mage Training: Mages train by inscribing Rune Stars into their hearts — each circle is a new sigil burned into cardiac tissue by Veyn. The process is excruciatingly painful and must be completed step by step. Skipping circles causes instant death. Between inscriptions, Mages practice spell shaping — learning to mentally form the patterns required for each skill. A typical Mage trains for 2-3 years before their first inscription.

Bladesinger Training: Bladesingers train through repetitive sword forms — thousands of repetitions of each strike, parry, and movement until they become instinctive. Training begins with wooden swords and progresses to steel, then to Veyn-infused practice blades. The goal is to make swordplay as natural as breathing.

Berserker Training: Berserkers train by pushing their bodies to physical limits — lifting increasingly heavy weights, running until exhaustion, and fighting in controlled bouts. Their training emphasizes overwhelming force and pain tolerance. Berserkers learn to channel Ren through sheer willpower, which requires conditioning their bodies to handle the strain.

Paladin Training: Paladins train in both combat and healing. They practice sword forms like Bladesingers but also practice meditation to refine their Auric Ren. The dual focus makes Paladin training the longest — typically 5-7 years before a Paladin is considered combat-ready.

Veilrunner Training: Veilrunners train in stealth, silence, and precision. They practice moving through obstacle courses without making sound, picking locks, and striking targets from hiding. The final test is infiltrating a guarded building and stealing an object without being detected.

fields.value: Rune Star inscriptions into heart — excruciating, step by step, 2-3 years per circle

name: Dojo & Training Grounds
subtitle: Where fighters practice across the realms
description:
Every realm has dedicated spaces for combat training.

The Ashwell Arena: The Human Realm's premier combat venue. A massive circular colosseum in the capital that seats 10,000 spectators. Fighters compete in regulated bouts for prize money and reputation. The arena has Veyn-dampening barriers to prevent collateral damage. Tournament brackets are organized by grade — F-rank fighters compete separately from D-rank fighters.

The Obsidian Arena: The Demon Realm's equivalent — a brutal open-air arena carved from obsidian. No rules, no dampening barriers, no safety measures. Fighters compete until one is dead or yields. The arena hosts both combat sports and executions. The Mordrach watches from a raised platform above the arena floor.

Academy Training Grounds: The Academy has multiple training facilities — indoor sparring halls with Veyn-dampening wards, outdoor fields for large-scale exercises, and the Thornlost Forest for survival training. Students train in these spaces daily under Instructor supervision.

Pallantine Skyriding Fields: Open meadows in the Arubian Forest where Pallantine Elves practice Griffen-mounted combat. Skyriding tournaments involve aerial obstacle courses, target shooting from Griffen-back, and formation flying drills.

Broker's Guild Sparring Rooms: Private training spaces within Guild offices where Brokers practice defensive techniques. Brokers are not fighters, but they learn basic self-defense and Veyn detection to protect themselves during dangerous negotiations.

name: Merchant Culture
subtitle: How traders operate across the realms
description:
Merchants are the economic backbone of the Human Realm and the primary connectors between realms.

Merchant Guilds: Every major city has a Merchant Guild — a regulatory body that oversees trade practices, resolves disputes between merchants, and negotiates with Magistrates on trade policy. Guild membership is required to operate a legitimate business in most cities. Membership costs 5-10 Gold Crowns annually.

Caravan Culture: Long-distance trade is conducted by caravans — groups of merchants and their guards traveling together for safety. A typical caravan includes 5-20 merchants, 10-30 guards, pack animals, and supplies for the journey. Caravans follow established routes and stop at waystations along the way.

Haggling: Haggling is expected and respected in the Human Realm. A merchant who accepts the first offer is considered a fool; a customer who doesn't haggle is considered naive. The Demon Realm has no haggling — prices are fixed and arguing results in violence. The Angel Realm has no commerce in the traditional sense — trade is conducted through Vow-based exchange.

Merchant Intelligence: Smart merchants maintain networks of contacts across realms — innkeepers, tavern keepers, port officials, and other merchants who share information about market conditions, supply shortages, and political changes. This intelligence network is separate from the Broker's Guild but overlaps significantly.

Merchant Ethics: The Merchant Guild enforces ethical standards — price gouging during emergencies is fined, selling counterfeit goods results in expulsion, and exploiting new merchants is socially punished. The worst offense is selling corrupted Veyn artifacts to unsuspecting buyers — this results in permanent exile from the Guild.

fields.value: Regulatory bodies in every major city — 5-10gc annual membership

name: The Broker's Daily Life
subtitle: What a working Broker actually does
description:
Brokers are not just contract managers — they are information hubs, negotiators, and problem solvers.

A typical Broker's day: Morning — review pending contracts, meet with clients to discuss terms, draft new agreements. Afternoon — attend to disputes, mediate between parties, enforce contract terms. Evening — meet with informants, gather intelligence, attend social events where deals are made informally.

The Broker's most important tool is their network — contacts in every realm, every class, every profession. A well-connected Broker knows who needs what, who has what, and who is willing to trade. This information is their most valuable asset.

Broker Ethics: Brokers must remain neutral in all disputes they mediate. Taking sides results in certification revocation. Brokers cannot refuse service based on race, class, or realm — a Broker who refuses to mediate a contract between a human and a demon loses their license.

Broker Safety: Brokers deal with dangerous people — demons, criminals, desperate merchants. Self-defense training is mandatory for certification. Many Brokers carry concealed weapons and wear Wraithcloth for protection. The Broker's Guild provides legal representation if a Broker is threatened or attacked.

Broker Advancement: Brokers advance based on the value and complexity of contracts they handle. A junior Broker handles small trade agreements; a senior Broker handles realm-spanning deals worth millions of Gold Crowns. The most powerful Brokers advise rulers and negotiate between realms.

fields.value: Morning: contracts and clients; Afternoon: disputes and mediation; Evening: informants and social

fields.label: Most Valuable Tool
fields.value: Information network — contacts in every realm, class, profession

fields.label: Neutrality Rule
fields.value: Taking sides = certification revocation; cannot refuse service based on race/class/realm
